title: CT's $50M supply chain incentive program fuels manufacturing expansions
description:
The Strategic Supply Chain Initiative, or SSCI, is a relatively new development incentive administered by Connecticut’s Department of Economic and Community Development.
ADVERTISEMENT The state initially allocated $25 million in grants for the program and added another $25 million in early 2026, bringing its total funding to $50 million.
ADVERTISEMENT The state funding is intended to generate substantially larger private investments.
Regional President Jim Hickson said programs such as SSCI are important to companies operating in Connecticut’s portion of the aerospace manufacturing corridor known as Aerospace Alley.
PDS Director of Business Development Paul Borawski said his firm is seeing an overall uptick in demand for manufacturing facilities in Connecticut.
text:
When aerospace contract manufacturer Ramar-Hall broke ground on a $5 million expansion of its Middlefield facility in late August, the ceremony also marked the public debut of the second funding round under Connecticut’s Strategic Supply Chain Initiative.

Backed by a $700,000 forgivable state loan, Ramar-Hall will add 15,000 square feet of manufacturing space to its current 30,000-square-foot facility, and create at least 10 high-paying jobs.

The Strategic Supply Chain Initiative, or SSCI, is a relatively new development incentive administered by Connecticut’s Department of Economic and Community Development. It was conceived in late 2024 amid expectations that the incoming Trump administration would impose sweeping tariffs that could prompt manufacturers to move more production back to the United States.

The program is designed to support companies that play important roles in the supply chains of Connecticut’s core industries, including aerospace and defense, semiconductors, financial technology, life sciences, clean energy and information technology.

ADVERTISEMENT

The state initially allocated $25 million in grants for the program and added another $25 million in early 2026, bringing its total funding to $50 million. The second round provides forgivable loans instead of grants, giving Connecticut greater leverage to ensure recipients meet their investment and hiring commitments, said Connecticut Chief Manufacturing Officer Kirti Patel.

Ten projects have been approved in the second round and are in various stages of negotiation, according to DECD. Ramar-Hall is the first to be publicly announced.

“We’re looking for companies that are looking to reshore operations, relocate to Connecticut, but also companies that already have a presence in Connecticut but are expanding production capacity,” Patel said. “It needs to move the needle on the state’s GDP, including also the net revenue to the state.”

In other words, companies seeking funds to simply update equipment or operations without expansion will not qualify. Instead, Patel said projects must hold significant potential to increase production, sales and employment, although there are no set parameters for individual deals.

ADVERTISEMENT

Applicants submit projected capital spending and the number of jobs they expect to create over 10 years. DECD then uses an economic model to estimate the project’s potential return to the state and determine the appropriate incentive, Patel said.

Companies may apply for awards ranging from $500,000 to $5 million.

The first $25 million has been fully committed to about 24 projects, 15 of which have been publicly announced. Hanwha Aerospace, Trumpf and GKN Aerospace received the largest awards, at $2.5 million each.

When the awards were announced in 2025, state officials said Trumpf would use the funding to add a press-brake production line at its Farmington headquarters and create 63 jobs. GKN’s award was intended to help establish a 3D-printing operation at its Newington plant, bringing production performed in Sweden to Connecticut and adding about 20 employees.

ADVERTISEMENT

The state funding is intended to generate substantially larger private investments. Companies selected during the first round have committed to spend a combined $350 million and create 650 jobs, Patel said.

Businesses that do not qualify for the supply chain program may be directed to DECD’s Manufacturing Innovation Fund, which offers incentives of up to $100,000 for equipment purchases and other upgrades.

Running out of room

Ramar-Hall, which recently celebrated its 70th anniversary, manufactures aerospace components for customers that include Pratt & Whitney and Collins Aerospace, both RTX businesses, and Triumph Aerospace in West Hartford.

“We’re getting a lot of new business opportunities and we’ve been fortunate to get a higher percentage of contracts than we typically expect, and so because of that, we’re basically running out of space,” said George Monahan, the company’s director of quality and operations.

Ramar-Hall had already expanded by acquisition. In January 2024, it bought Hamden-based The Durol Co., which had complementary operations. Ramar-Hall continues to operate Durol’s 10,000-square-foot Hamden facility with seven employees.

Ramar-Hall has close to 50 employees at its main Middlefield facility.

Monahan said negotiations for the Middlefield expansion began with AdvanceCT, the state’s nonprofit business recruitment arm, which identified the SSCI program as a potential fit and helped the company through the application process.

Ramar-Hall’s longtime lender, Beacon Bank, is providing another $2 million toward the project. Regional President Jim Hickson said programs such as SSCI are important to companies operating in Connecticut’s portion of the aerospace manufacturing corridor known as Aerospace Alley.

“The company was able to access more capital — more debt to facilitate their growth — by using the DECD as part of the equation,” Hickson told the Hartford Business Journal. “It does help lower the cost of a company’s capital.”

Monahan described the application process as extensive but said the state funding allowed Ramar-Hall to accelerate an expansion it already planned to pursue.

“We would have gone ahead without a doubt because it needed to be done in order for us to respond to the request of our customers and the long-term forecast that we’re seeing,” he said. “The state just allowed us to accelerate that and make this happen faster.”

More to come

Site preparation for the expansion is underway with Bloomfield’s PDS Engineering and Construction taking the lead. The company expects to enclose the new structure before winter and complete construction in the spring.

PDS Director of Business Development Paul Borawski said his firm is seeing an overall uptick in demand for manufacturing facilities in Connecticut.

“We’re ​looking ​forward ​to ​obviously ​helping ​them ​grow ​​so ​they ​can ​help ​support ​the ​aerospace ​industry,” he said of Ramar-Hall. “They ​have ​the ​state ​support ​on ​this, so ​I ​think ​this ​is ​going ​to ​be ​one ​of ​many ​to ​come ​in ​the ​near ​future.”

Patel said additional SSCI awards are expected to be announced soon, potentially including the first involving a company relocating to Connecticut.

text:
ACEA call for delay to EV rules as UK-EU trade faces 10% tariff

European carmakers are calling for a further delay to tougher rules of origin for electric vehicles, warning that a failure to act could expose large numbers of vehicles traded between the UK and EU to a 10% tariff from 1 January 2027.

The warning, reported by the Financial Times, comes as manufacturers continue to rely heavily on batteries and other key electric vehicle components sourced from outside Europe, particularly China. The European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) has subsequently confirmed that it has written to EU leaders seeking a temporary change to the battery rules of origin contained in the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA).

The issue is particularly significant for the UK automotive industry because Britain is outside the EU single market. While the TCA allows qualifying vehicles to be traded between the UK and EU without customs tariffs, vehicles must meet increasingly stringent rules of origin requirements to benefit from that preferential treatment.

From 1 January 2027, the requirements are due to become substantially tougher. Under the existing agreement, an electric vehicle will need to meet a 55% UK/EU content threshold, while its battery pack will need to meet a 70% originating-content requirement and battery cells a 65% threshold. Vehicles that fail the applicable requirements can face a 10% customs tariff when crossing the UK-EU border.

Carmakers seek another delay

The UK and EU had already agreed in December 2023 to postpone the next stage of the rules of origin regime. The tougher requirements originally scheduled for 1 January 2024 were instead deferred until the end of 2026, giving manufacturers additional time to establish battery production and develop regional supply chains.

At the time, the UK Government said the extension would help the industry scale up domestic battery production and avoid the imposition of 10% tariffs on electric vehicle trade.

However, ACEA now argues that the European battery supply chain has not developed quickly enough to enable manufacturers to meet the 2027 requirements.

In its 17 September letter, ACEA said the rules due to apply from January 2027 “cannot be met by European vehicle manufacturers”. The organisation is proposing that the more flexible treatment of battery packs should remain in place until the end of 2029, followed by stricter requirements for battery cells from 2030 and cathode materials from 2032.

ACEA says the objective is not to abandon localisation requirements, but to align their introduction with the speed at which the European battery industry is actually developing.

The organisation says manufacturers have already made significant investments in European battery production, but the full capacity resulting from those investments will only become available over the coming years.

ACEA argues that “the question is not whether they will be able to comply, but when”, adding that EU trade policy should be aligned with the pace of Europe’s industrial policy on localisation.

£1.5bn annual tariff risk

The potential financial impact is substantial.

ACEA estimates that the EU could export around 520,000 electric passenger cars and vans to the UK in 2027, with a combined value of approximately €17.9bn. Under the rules currently scheduled to apply, it estimates that 82% of those exports would fail to meet the rules of origin requirements and would consequently face the 10% customs duty.

ACEA estimates that this could generate around €1.47bn in additional customs costs in 2027 alone.

The FT report places the issue in the wider context of European automotive trade, with the same rules applying in the opposite direction to UK-built electric vehicles exported into the EU.

That creates a particular problem for UK manufacturers whose vehicles contain batteries or battery components sourced from China or other countries outside the UK and EU. The rules do not simply consider where the vehicle is assembled. They also determine whether sufficient value within the vehicle and its battery originates within the qualifying trading area.

UK-made EVs that fail to meet the relevant rules could therefore lose tariff-free access to the EU market and face a 10% import duty.

For manufacturers operating on tight margins, the tariff could either increase the cost of vehicles for customers or have to be absorbed by manufacturers, potentially affecting the economics of production and exports.

Why batteries are at the centre of the problem

Batteries are particularly important because they account for a significant proportion of the value of an electric vehicle and remain one of the areas in which Europe is heavily dependent on overseas supply chains.

The UK Government’s own battery strategy previously highlighted the importance of establishing domestic production to meet the TCA requirements. It noted that batteries account for approximately 40% of the cost of a car and that dependence on imported batteries could make it harder for UK manufacturers to satisfy rules of origin requirements.

The challenge is not simply battery cell production. The supply chain extends through cathode materials, active materials, battery modules, packs and other components.

That means a vehicle can be assembled in Britain or the EU while still containing substantial non-originating content.

China remains particularly important to the global battery supply chain. This has created a difficult balancing act for European manufacturers: they are being encouraged to localise production and reduce strategic dependencies while simultaneously being expected to meet rules that assume a sufficiently developed regional supply chain already exists.

ACEA’s proposal is therefore aimed at providing additional time for European battery investments to reach commercial scale.

EU wants more “Made in Europe” production

The dispute comes against the backdrop of a wider EU push to strengthen domestic industrial capacity.

In March 2026, the European Commission proposed its Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), designed to increase demand for European-made and low-carbon products and technologies. The proposal covers strategic sectors including cars and net-zero technologies such as batteries.

The Commission says the IAA is intended to strengthen European production capacity, reduce dependencies on non-EU suppliers and create greater demand for European manufacturing.

It proposes “Made in EU” and low-carbon requirements in areas including public procurement and public support schemes, while also seeking to attract investment and accelerate the development of industrial projects.

The Commission says manufacturing represented 14.3% of EU GDP in 2024 and has set a goal of increasing the manufacturing share to 20% by 2035.

The IAA remains a legislative proposal rather than an adopted law, and it is being negotiated by the European Parliament and Council.

ACEA has broadly supported the objective of strengthening Europe’s industrial base. In May, it said the automotive sector recognised the need to build an integrated European battery value chain, while warning that the assumptions underpinning some of the proposed measures were optimistic.

This creates an important distinction for the UK automotive sector. The IAA’s “Made in EU” provisions are part of a broader industrial policy, while the immediate 10% tariff threat from January 2027 stems from the separate EU-UK TCA rules of origin.

Nevertheless, the two policies are connected by the same strategic objective: increasing the amount of automotive and battery production taking place within Europe.

European battery investment has fallen short

The problem for manufacturers is that investment has not translated into sufficient available capacity quickly enough.

ACEA’s request follows a period in which several European battery projects have encountered financial and operational difficulties. The FT highlighted the collapse of Northvolt as one example of the challenges facing Europe’s emerging battery industry, while weaker-than-expected EV demand has also affected investment decisions.

At the same time, European manufacturers remain under pressure from Chinese EV producers, which benefit from much deeper battery supply chains and substantial economies of scale.

The EU has already introduced countervailing duties on Chinese battery electric vehicles, while its industrial strategy is increasingly focused on strengthening domestic production and reducing strategic dependencies.

The resulting policy challenge is complex. Rules of origin are intended to encourage investment in European battery manufacturing, but manufacturers argue that enforcing them before sufficient European capacity exists could impose substantial costs on the very companies being asked to invest.

What it means for UK fleets and manufacturers

For UK fleet operators, the immediate consequences would be indirect but potentially significant.

If the 10% tariff is applied to UK-built EVs that fail to meet the rules of origin, manufacturers could face higher costs when supplying the EU. The impact could influence production decisions, vehicle pricing and the allocation of models between UK and European markets.

The UK is an important manufacturing base for vehicles destined for Europe, while the EU is also a major source of vehicles and components for the UK market. Consequently, the rules have implications beyond individual vehicle manufacturers.

For fleet operators considering electric vehicle procurement, changes in supply chains and vehicle pricing could also affect model availability and total acquisition costs.

The issue is particularly relevant to manufacturers with UK production operations that rely on imported batteries. Even where final vehicle assembly takes place in Britain, the origin of the battery and its components can determine whether the finished vehicle qualifies for tariff-free trade.

The TCA rules were specifically designed to encourage UK and EU investment in battery manufacturing. The fact that manufacturers are now asking for another delay demonstrates the difficulty of building an entirely regional EV supply chain within the original timetable.

A decision with implications beyond tariffs

ACEA’s proposal is effectively asking policymakers to choose between maintaining the scheduled timetable for localisation and allowing manufacturers more time to develop the supply chain needed to comply.

The association is not seeking to remove the long-term localisation requirements. Instead, it wants battery pack assembly to remain the basis for the rules until the end of 2029, followed by tighter requirements for battery cells from 2030 and cathode materials from 2032

The proposal therefore represents a further attempt to bridge the gap between Europe’s industrial ambitions and the current state of its EV supply chain.

For the UK, the stakes are particularly high because a failure to satisfy the rules could directly affect tariff-free access to the EU’s automotive market. For European manufacturers, the issue works in both directions, with ACEA warning that tariffs on EU-built EVs entering the UK could undermine competitiveness and market share.

The European Commission and EU member states must now consider whether the 2027 rules should proceed as planned or whether another transitional arrangement is required.

With the January 2027 deadline approaching, the outcome will be closely watched across the automotive industry. It could determine not only the cost of UK-EU EV trade, but also how quickly manufacturers are able to shift towards a genuinely European battery supply chain.

text:
It’s perhaps unsurprising to discover that the founder of a company named after a rather obscure Latin word (metris, meaning to measure) is an Oxford graduate.

But Oxford was only Natasha Jones’ first degree. Her second - a Master of Science - is about as far removed from ancient languages as you can get. Though it did provide the momentum to set up her London-headquartered company, Metris Energy, in 2023 – just a few years after becoming a first-class MSc degree holder.

Today, September 21, Jones is celebrating some big news: her AI-native platform for managing energy assets at scale has raised a $5 million seed round, led by PT1 Ventures, Octopus Ventures, AENU and Blackfinch Ventures, with participation from Plug and Play and Love Ventures.

Like her AI-powered software, Jones is all about the data. And the lack of joined-up thinking in the energy sector when it comes to data is precisely the gap she’s aiming to fill. “Energy asset data lives in many places and none of them agree. That’s the problem we’re tackling by creating a living system of record of energy projects,” she begins.

One of Jones’ recent LinkedIn posts regarding her fast-moving expansion into the German market puts this point into even sharper focus. “Germany has more distributed solar than any other market in Europe. Most of it is still managed in spreadsheets,” she observed.

The Metris metrics

Jones says Metris began by solving a “single, painful problem” for solar portfolios: reconciling data scattered across inverters, meters, SCADA, CRMs, spreadsheets and finance tools into one clean, reliable record. And she reveals how that focus has since evolved into a broader ambition to become the unified data layer for the entire energy sector.

The founder and CEO cites four key things she’s learned about energy asset data on her journey so far. “The first is that asset identity isn't fixed. Equipment gets swapped out, sites get re-registered, portfolios get traded. Treat your asset register as static and eventually you'll book revenue against a device that hasn't even been installed yet.

“Secondly, ‘generation’ isn't one number. Inverter output, meter export, deemed generation under curtailment – these are all different things and mixing them up matters.”

She says the third lesson learned is that "a zero doesn't mean one thing". “It could be night, a comms dropout, a failed inverter or active curtailment. Fill that gap silently and you've just deleted the alarm that was telling you an asset is down,” Jones explains.

The fourth lesson she notes is that “the unglamorous work is the moat".

"Unifying hundreds of vendor integrations into one flexible model is complex and tedious for human-led teams, but it's what actually makes the difference with automation.”

And bringing automation into a sector that’s so ripe to reap its benefits is precisely where her focus is. Today’s funding news comes alongside the launch of Metria AI, the company’s new AI interface that Jones says is designed to “seamlessly execute complex tasks previously carried out manually by operations teams".

Jones explains that Metria AI takes its name from that same Latin suffix as Metris, “but integrates IA, the European abbreviation for AI”.

Management layer

Jones has long bemoaned the fact there isn’t a unified layer that lets asset owners – or indeed the AI agents now entering this space – actually see and act on their portfolio. And this issue is becoming more pressing as those portfolios increasingly combine the likes of solar, wind, storage and flexible demand. So, how could her proposed unified data and AI layer change the way operators capture value from assets?

“Firstly, in reconciling behind-the-meter (BTM) and front-of-the meter (FTM) flexibility. In the commercial and industrial segment, no one has managed to bring BTM and FTM flexibility together into a single, holistic view of energy and savings/revenue – Metris can unify this through our data and partner integrations,” says Jones emphatically.

She also flags her platform’s potential for identifying new operational prospects: “We can pinpoint the various up-and-coming opportunities for repowering assets, battery installation and tariff optimisation across a portfolio, so that asset owners can begin taking advantage of them.”

But the biggest missed opportunity in the current status quo, in Jones’ view? “Asset owners and managers currently spend around 80% of their time collecting, checking and compiling data, and only 20% analysing it for insights that inform performance management and future development. Metris flips that 80/20 split,” she states.

Disruptive technology

Naturally, given both her company’s AI focus and the engrained legacy methods she’s trying to encourage cautious operators to replace, Jones is well versed in answering questions about potential safety issues. But she’s keen to point out that, despite the application of AI here, the human remains very much in the loop.

“Metria AI draws information from across the platform to predict fault diagnosis and repair: energy data, fault codes, OEM manuals, project info and historic tickets. This cuts hours of times from monitoring teams who would typically have to dive into multiple charts, tickets and hidden documents to get answers and then manually generate workorders,” Jones details.

“Metria does this automatically and our intelligence continuously improves over time as predictions are approved or edited, more site context is uploaded onto the platform and final O&M site reports verify ‘on-the-ground’ truth.”

In any case, she observes: “Today, the system is advisory only: no action is ever taken on a live portfolio without explicit operator approval, allowing total user control on work orders undertaken on site.”

Investment opportunity

The industry response to Jones’s work suggests that, despite any AI naysayers, people very much 'get' what she’s trying to achieve. Its latest raise brings the company’s funding thus far to $7.5 million. Metris has seen eight times revenue growth year-on-year and the platform already manages more than 10,000 solar plants and 500MW of capacity for some of the largest power producers in the world. These are all pretty astonishing figures for such a young company, but its ambitious founder is keen to emphasise that this is only the beginning.

When asked how this latest funding will be put to work. Jones’ three-point answer illustrates her considered approach to scaling up. Interestingly, for a software company CEO, she mentions hardware first.

“Hardware partnerships will form a key part of our next steps. We're expanding our partnerships programme with hardware providers to offer customers an end-to-end solution – best-in-class-devices paired with best-in-class-data processing and aggregation,” is how she describes this vision.

Battery energy storage systems applications are next on her list. Jones comments: “BESS is increasingly important for German solar players and the funding allows us to develop our BESS capabilities further. We also have existing customers who are expanding into Germany alongside us.”

Finally, she’s also planning a platform expansion into new areas. “The funding enables us to extend the platform to cover wind and CHP too. Customers increasingly want a single platform that aggregates all power production in one place and we'll be able to provide that,” Jones confirms.

Ultimately, for Jones, everything comes back to the data. “We live and die by the quality of our data and how we translate that into KPIs our customers care about – hence the name ‘Metris’,” she says.

“Admittedly, we do also enjoy the name’s nod to everyone’s favourite arcade game, Tetris, as it nicely illustrates how all of our data slots perfectly together,” Jones adds with a smile.

text:
LANSING - There are more than 40 air quality monitors across Michigan operated by the Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy, but only two in the Upper Peninsula.

And that raises serious public health concerns due to an increasing number of wildfires and the smoke that follows, environmental experts say.

"Particulate matter can penetrate deep into lungs, and wildfire smoke exposure is an immediate acute event," said Samantha Pickering, the public and environmental health policy manager at the Michigan Environmental Council.

One is at the Seney National Wildlife Refuge in the Eastern UP. In 2024, the second monitor was added outside of Marquette's city limits.

The two monitors in the UP check for different pollutants. One measures PM 2.5 pollutants, which are small particles like liquid droplets or tiny solid 2.5 micrometers of chemicals.

There are no current plans to add more monitors in the UP, according to the department's website.

"When you get closer to the southeast side of the state, that's where you see the majority of them." For example, the large amount of industry and how dense the population is in Detroit makes air quality monitoring a priority, compared to less populated areas in the state, Pickering said.

The goal is to increase the monitoring capacity, although funding is an issue, she said.

"They're very costly," she said. "Not all rural communities are accurately represented currently in monitoring and data collection."

According to a 2024 posting on the Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy website, "Citizens have asked for more air quality monitoring in the UP for many years."

Organizations like the American Lung Association and local UP health departments emphasize the danger of these air pollutants, especially for those in rural areas who work outdoors or lack clean air shelter.

People such as elders and children, especially ones with asthma and other chronic diseases, are highly negatively impacted by the smoke, health experts say.

If particles are breathed in it can cause people to miss days of work and school and may cause long or short-term health risks, such as heart attacks and premature deaths for those with existing respiratory illnesses, according to the Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy.

Pickering said research has also shown adverse effects of wildfire smoke on mental health and on glaucoma patients.

In addition, she said, "There's a big role that socioeconomics plays in this, since it's hard to get access to resources in rural areas, such as medical care."

Low-income people who cannot access protective equipment or air filtering equipment are at a bigger risk for negative health impacts, according to the Michigan Department of Health & Human Services.

The impact on animals from air pollutants and wildfire smoke hasn't been researched well enough, Pickering said.

"We do know though, that smoke can lead to dairy cows producing less milk," she said.

text:
LG Energy Solution has completed the establishment of its energy storage system (ESS) production network in North America, accelerating its push to capture growing demand in the rapidly expanding ESS market.

Following the opening ceremony for LG Energy Solution Michigan-Lansing on Aug. 18, the plant is now ramping up operations.

The Lansing plant serves as a combined manufacturing hub for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for ESS applications and nickel cobalt manganese batteries for electric vehicles (EVs), with an annual battery cell production capacity of more than 35 gigawatt-hours.

The plant began producing pouch-type LFP batteries for ESS applications this year and plans to begin mass production of prismatic LFP batteries next year, marking LG Energy Solution's first prismatic battery production in North America. The company has also secured orders to supply EV batteries to Toyota.

LG Energy Solution Michigan operates two production sites in the state, in Holland and Lansing. LG Energy Solution Michigan President Choi Dae-sik said that operating two plants in different locations is not easy but “there is significant synergy because we can quickly transfer the experience accumulated at the existing plant to the new one.”

He said the company is transferring its production and quality management experience and operational know-how from Holland to Lansing to accelerate the stabilization of the new plant and minimize trial and error. The company plans to connect the workforce, organizations and production experience of the two plants to operate them as a single production system.

With the Lansing plant going into operation, LG Energy Solution now has five ESS manufacturing sites in North America: two in Michigan, NextStar Energy’s plant in Ontario, Canada, and two joint venture plants — L-H Battery Company’s plant in Ohio and Ultium Cells’ plant in Tennessee.

By the end of this year, LG Energy Solution plans to expand its ESS production capacity in North America to 50 gigawatt-hours, accounting for 80 percent of its global ESS production capacity. Based on the improved capacity, the company said it will meet rapidly growing demand in the region.

LG Energy Solution’s ESS order backlog reached 140 gigawatt-hours as of the end of last year, while it secured more than 3 trillion won ($2.17 billion) in new ESS orders in the first half of this year.

LG Energy Solution has signed a series of supply deals with customers including Tesla, Terra-Gen, Excelsior Energy Capital, EG4 Electronics and Hanwha Qcells.

In May, LG Energy Solution signed a 6 gigawatt-hour ESS battery supply deal with DTE Energy, which is involved in Oracle’s artificial intelligence data center project. In July, it agreed to supply up to 2.9 gigawatt-hours of ESS batteries for a Google project with renewable energy independent power producer Cypress Creek Energy.

“The operation at Lansing plant is an important milestone that will accelerate LG Energy Solution’s growth in North America,” LG Energy Solution CEO Kim Dong-myung said. “We will strengthen the U.S. battery ecosystem and expand our local production capabilities by building an advanced battery manufacturing network that supports the future of the U.S. mobility industry and energy infrastructure.” (Advertorial)

text:
Carbon fiber is a key component in automobile manufacturing, aerospace engineering and energy infrastructure, but it mostly relies on petroleum-derived products, which can be expensive and contribute to carbon emissions. But what if carbon fiber was made of a free waste material and was as strong as - or even stronger than - the petrochemical-based products? Engineers at Washington University in St. Louis are unveiling that prospect in research recently published in the journal Matter.

“For the first time, this allows us to create renewable carbon fiber that reaches the high standard of quality used in automobile manufacturing,” said Joshua Yuan, the Lucy & Stanley Lopata Professor and chair of energy, environmental and chemical engineering at WashU McKelvey Engineering. Yuan is also the director of the National Science Foundation (NSF) Carbon Utilization Redesign for Biomanufacturing (CURB) Engineering Research Center at WashU.

Key to the work is making use of a waste material called lignin, the second-most abundant natural biopolymer on earth. Lignin is produced as a byproduct of the paper pulping and biorefining industries, and ordinary disposal methods for lignin result in a substantial environmental footprint.

WashU engineers wanted to see if they could use lignin to improve production methods for carbon fiber. This human-made material is traditionally manufactured using synthetic polyacrylonitrile (PAN), a petroleum-derived product that is mixed with chemicals, spun through tiny jets into fibers, washed and stretched. This type of production process for carbon fiber is called "wet spinning." However, PAN is not cheap, accounting for up to 50% of the total manufacturing cost of carbon fibers, which limits its use to high-end products, Yuan noted.

By adding affordable and abundant lignin to the process, the WashU team found that they could cut the use of PAN by half, reduce production costs by 25% and cut carbon emissions substantially. But the new carbon-fiber product they created still needed to meet automobile industry standards for tensile strength and elastic modulus.

So the researchers also developed another new process that greatly improves performance. That process involves deploying single-walled carbon nanotubes into the polymer matrix, acting almost like rebar in lining up the crystallization chemistry. This innovation revealed a new design principle for carbon material development.

“Crystallization alignment is critical for carbon fiber quality,” Yuan said.

The carbon nanotubes allowed the researchers to make a precursor solution of the lignin and PAN. That solution was then extruded as fiber for the wet spinning process of production, then further heat-treated to strengthen the product.

Weiwei Li, a postdoctoral scholar in Yuan's lab and first author of the research, described their research as an innovation in three steps.

The first step was to create that nanotube template that can mix well with lignin and PAN and allows for high crystallization or orientation, Li said. Step two involves running that precursor solution through a wet spinning and tension-assisted heat treatment. Finally, one round of optimized carbonization fully strengthens the fiber. The three steps together maximized the crystallite content, while the carbon nanotubes guide the crystallite orientation to create rebar effects for outstanding mechanical properties.

“All these together allow us to create lignin-based renewable carbon fiber that has highly aligned crystalline structure,” Yuan said.

The automobile industry is just the entry point for markets of optimized carbon fiber; it's used in many industries, from sports equipment to wind turbines.

“Carbon fiber reinforces plastics and has very broad application,” Yuan said.

text:
Staff Reporter

PRESIDENT Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah has called for a clean energy transition that is measured not only in megawatts and emissions, but in jobs, skills and industrial value created for developing countries.

Speaking in New York on Saturday on the occasion of the United Nations Private Sector Forum hosted by the UN Global Compact under the theme “Advancing a Clean, Just and Secure Energy Future”, the President said energy policy has become inseparable from economic security, climate resilience and human development.

“We meet at a moment when energy policy has become inseparable from economic security, climate resilience and human development. The question before us is no longer whether the global energy system must change, but how we can accelerate that change at the scale and pace required,” Nandi-Ndaitwah said.

Photos: Namibian Presidency

She said for Namibia, the energy debate is not abstract, as reliable and affordable energy determines whether a rural clinic can preserve medicines, whether a small enterprise can expand, and whether a young person can find decent work at home.

“A clean energy transition must therefore be measured not only in megawatts installed or emissions avoided, but in jobs created, communities connected, skills transferred and industries established,” she said.

Nandi-Ndaitwah said Namibia supports the objectives of the Paris Agreement and limiting global temperature increase to 1.5 degrees Celsius, but stressed that the transition must recognise different national circumstances and safeguard the right of developing countries to industrialise, eradicate poverty and secure universal energy access.

“A transition that leaves communities without power, workers without viable alternatives or countries trapped at the bottom of global value chains will neither be durable nor fair,” she warned.

She said Namibia’s approach is anchored in a diversified energy system, expanded domestic generation and stronger regional integration.

At continental level, she said Africa’s energy transition must be an industrialisation strategy that uses clean energy not only to export electricity or unprocessed minerals, but to manufacture, beneficiate, strengthen food systems, modernise transport and create a skilled workforce.

Nandi-Ndaitwah said governments must provide direction, predictability and enabling infrastructure, while business must bring investment, innovation and responsible execution. She called on the UN, development finance institutions and international partners to help align standards, mobilise finance and strengthen cooperation.

“Together, we can build an energy future that is cleaner and more secure; an industrial future that creates value where resources are found; and a transition that is genuinely inclusive and leaves no country, community or worker behind,” she said, adding that young people and women must play a central role.

She invited business leaders to join Namibia in the journey towards a cleaner, healthier and more prosperous world.

The event was attended by UN Secretary-General António Guterres, UN Global Compact CEO Sanda Ojiambo, Heads of State and Government, and private sector leaders.

text:
Market snapshot: Tube Investments of India's electric vehicle subsidiary, Montra Electric, has mapped out an aggressive roadmap to achieve a revenue of $1 billion (approximately ₹9,600 crore) by the year 2030. Under this plan, nearly 70% of the targeted top-line expansion will be driven by electric trucks. This marks a significant strategic pivot toward the commercial heavy and light vehicle segments as the primary engines of long-term growth.

Data Snapshot

Montra Electric is targeting a top-line milestone of ₹9,600 crore by 2030.

Electric trucks are projected to contribute nearly 70% of the target 2030 revenue.

Montra Electric recorded ₹740 crore in consolidated revenue for the previous financial year.

What's Changed

Targeting a ≈13x revenue multiplier to reach ₹9,600 crore by 2030, compared to the recorded revenue of ₹740 crore in the preceding fiscal year (derived: ₹9,600 cr vs ₹740 cr).

Shift in product-mix focus with heavy electric trucks emerging as the primary revenue contributor at 50% of total targets, while three-wheelers shift to a 20% share.

Key Takeaways

Electric trucks will anchor the company's long-term commercial vehicle architecture, projected to bring in nearly ₹6,720 crore of the 2030 revenue target.

Heavy commercial vehicles will generate half of the target revenue, with small commercial vehicles contributing 23-25%.

The brand currently has approximately 21,000 active vehicles on the road across various segments.

Strategic emphasis is moving toward high-capacity battery solutions (350 to 400 kilowatts) to mitigate range limitations on short, predictable shipping routes.

SAHI Perspective

Montra Electric's 2030 roadmap points to a bold move away from lightweight passenger vehicles into capital-intensive electric trucking. Although electric truck penetration in India currently sits below 1% due to massive long-haul infrastructure deficits, the company is targeting predictable, closed-loop freight networks where battery capacity limits are manageable. Backed by its parent Tube Investments of India, which has injected and raised ₹3,000 crore for clean mobility operations, Montra possesses the financial leverage to build local manufacturing scale and battery systems.

Market Implications

Montra's expansion into electric commercial trucks intensifies competition in a high-tonnage vehicle market historically dominated by legacy players. Its focus on localization—exemplified by its 1.7 GWh battery assembly plant in Manesar—helps insulate the company from component supply shocks and enables better unit pricing, accelerating industrial transition timelines.

Trading Signals

Market Bias: Bullish

Tube Investments is well-positioned to benefit from its clean mobility arm's scale-up, backed by a clear ₹9,600 crore 2030 revenue target and high-value fleet partnerships such as the deployment of 57 heavy trucks with TVS Vehicle Mobility Solutions.

Overweight: Electric Vehicles, Auto Components, Commercial Vehicles

Underweight: Traditional ICE Components

Trigger Factors:

Sustained deployment of the Rhino series of heavy electric trucks across industrial routes.

Margin improvement driven by localized battery manufacturing at the Manesar facility.

Favorable policy clarity regarding PM E-Drive scheme scrapping linkages.

Time Horizon: Medium-term (3-12 months)

Industry Context

India's heavy commercial vehicle market is in the early stages of electrification. Because long-haul charging corridors remain limited, early adopters are relying on closed-loop logistics operations. Montra is targeting this specific segment, deploying fixed-battery and battery-swapping configurations to address range constraints and capture commercial fleet demand before highway charging networks fully mature.

Key Risks to Watch

Extremely low domestic market penetration (below 1%) of electric heavy commercial vehicles.

Lack of high-voltage charging networks along primary national transport highways.

Regulatory friction from PM E-Drive, which links purchasing subsidies to the voluntary scrapping of older diesel fleets.

Recent Developments

In August 2026, Montra Electric collaborated with TVS Vehicle Mobility Solutions (TVS VMS) to deploy 57 of its Rhino 5538 heavy electric commercial trucks into active freight services in Chhattisgarh. Concurrently, Montra expanded its operations internationally, entering new electric vehicle markets in Nepal, Tanzania, and West Africa.

Closing Insight

Montra's strategic direction highlights a structured transition from component fabrication to end-to-end commercial EV supply. Success in reaching its ₹9,600 crore revenue target will rest heavily on successfully scaling its localized battery operations and resolving range constraints through dedicated fleet partnerships.

text:
Commissioners Bill Brawley, Tommy Tucker and Donald van der Vaart say the $584 million project is premature, given what they see as unreliable estimates of future power demand. It’s certain that the project will put costs on the back of Duke’s ratepayers and pose “a significant risk that new generation is approved before the need for” it is clear, they said.

In a 3-1 decision, they opposed acting on the application before ruling on Duke’s updated Carolinas Resource Plan, the utility’s master plan for power-plant construction.

Van der Vaart said in a separate comment that the commission is under no obligation to green-light the projects in an approved resource plan.

Permit requests, he says, “must stand on [their] own evidentiary record” and the existence of the Carolinas Resource Plan “should not transform a subsequent [permit review] into a ministerial act.”

He also says 2025’s Senate Bill 266 requires Duke to show the Utilities Commission it has thought about whether it could blunt the need for new power plants through grid upgrades, conservation or power “storage.” The latter takes in battery storage and hydro systems like Duke’s Bad Creek plant in South Carolina.

Asserting that the turbine project was the only one Duke could bring on quickly “does not by itself substitute for” the work SB 266 requires, van der Vaart says.

The Sherwood Smith plant is next to the $10 billion data center Amazon plans in Richmond County.

Duke officials said they are “disappointed” by the ruling and are “assessing potential next steps.” Their studies showed the turbine was “part of a least-cost path to maintain reliable and affordable service for customers as energy demand continues to grow across North Carolina.”

The decision doesn’t tie the new turbine specifically to that project, but says that much of Duke’s power-demand projections are tied to data-center growth. Turbines such as the five at Sherwood Smith are generally peak-load units, not for around-the-clock use.

Friday’s decision came out as Duke was asking customers in the Carolinas to “voluntarily reduce electricity usage” from the afternoon into the early evening. “Above-average heat,” it said, was putting pressure on the grid.

Commissioner Floyd McKissick dissented from the decision, saying the added turbine would “provide critical firm capacity during extreme weather events” and other times “of elevated demand.”

“There is no Plan B,” he said, adding that there had been no opposition to the application.

Will Scott, a leader of the North Carolina branch of the Environmental Defense Fund, praised the ruling. Duke’s gas-plant build-out “is too rapid and too expensive,” and that short-term needs “should not saddle customers with what are, over the long-term, likely to be inefficient, stranded assets.”

Brawley, Tucker and van der Vaart are Republicans, while McKissick is a Democrat.

title: Public meeting set on formosa plastics wastewater permit | Local News - Crossroads Today
description:
The meeting comes as the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality considers Formosa’s application to renew the wastewater permit for its Point Comfort facility.
They are now questioning why the agency has taken a different position on Formosa’s permit.
San Antonio Bay Estuarine Waterkeeper and Environment Texas requested the October public meeting, giving residents an opportunity to raise concerns and provide comments on the proposed permit.
The public meeting begins at 7 p.m. Oct. 19 at the Bauer Community Center, 2300 State Highway 35 North in Port Lavaca.
The meeting will include an informal question-and-answer session with representatives from TCEQ and Formosa, followed by a formal public comment period.
text:
The meeting comes as the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality considers Formosa’s application to renew the wastewater permit for its Point Comfort facility.

Formosa proposed including a zero-discharge limit for plastic pellets, powders and flakes in the permit, consistent with requirements established under a federal court settlement. TCEQ instead proposed permit language that environmental groups say could allow an unspecified amount of plastic material to be discharged into Matagorda Bay.

Texas Surface Water Quality Standards require the state’s surface waters to be “essentially free” of floating debris and suspended solids that could harm aquatic life or interfere with the use and enjoyment of waterways.

Environmental groups say TCEQ previously indicated that the standard provided sufficient justification for zero-discharge requirements for plastics in individual wastewater permits. They are now questioning why the agency has taken a different position on Formosa’s permit.

“You know something’s backwards when the company is asking for a tougher pollution standard and the environmental agency won’t give it to them,” Environment Texas Executive Director Luke Metzger said. “TCEQ needs to explain its about-face and put a clear, enforceable zero-plastic-discharge limit in Formosa’s permit.”

In 2019, Formosa agreed to a $50 million settlement resolving a federal Clean Water Act lawsuit filed by San Antonio Bay Estuarine Waterkeeper and Diane Wilson. The lawsuit involved plastic pellets and other materials discharged from the Point Comfort complex into Cox Creek and Lavaca Bay. The settlement requires Formosa to stop discharging plastic pellets, powders and flakes and provides funding for environmental restoration and community projects.

San Antonio Bay Estuarine Waterkeeper and Environment Texas requested the October public meeting, giving residents an opportunity to raise concerns and provide comments on the proposed permit.

“Now is the time to show up, speak up and send a clear message to TCEQ to stop industrial plastic discharges into our bays and waterways,” San Antonio Bay Estuarine Waterkeeper Executive Director Diane Wilson said.

Wilson said the organization has documented plastic associated with Formosa’s wastewater discharges on 1,016 occasions since 2021.

The public meeting begins at 7 p.m. Oct. 19 at the Bauer Community Center, 2300 State Highway 35 North in Port Lavaca.

The meeting will include an informal question-and-answer session with representatives from TCEQ and Formosa, followed by a formal public comment period. Comments made during the formal portion will become part of TCEQ’s official record.

No final decision on the permit will be made at the meeting. The public comment period will close when the meeting concludes.

The permit application is available at the Port Lavaca Public Library, 200 W. Mahan St. TCEQ’s technical documents are also available online.

text:
LG Energy Solution has established five energy storage system (ESS) production sites across North America, accelerating its efforts to expand its presence in the rapidly growing ESS market. In August, the company held a grand opening ceremony for its new Lansing facility in Michigan with operations officially underway.

The start of production at the Lansing plant marks the completion of LG Energy Solution’s five-site ESS manufacturing network in North America. In response to the EV market slowdown and evolving clean energy policies, the company has strategically rebalanced its global production footprint by converting portions of EV battery production lines to ESS manufacturing. Through these efforts, LG Energy Solution has built one of the battery industry's most diversified manufacturing networks, positioning itself to meet rapidly increasing ESS demand across North America, driven by the expansion of data centers and renewable energy infrastructure.

The Lansing facility serves as a manufacturing hub capable of producing both LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries for ESS applications and NCM (nickel cobalt manganese) batteries for electric vehicles. The plant is expected to achieve an annual battery cell production capacity exceeding 35GWh. Production of ESS pouch cells began this year, while mass production of prismatic LFP batteries is scheduled to start next year. In its EV business, the company has also secured supply for Toyota.

With Lansing now operational, LG Energy Solution now operates five ESS production sites in North America, including three wholly owned facilities in Lansing and Holland, Michigan, and NextStar Energy in Ontario, Canada, as well as two joint venture plants: L-H Battery Company in Ohio and Ultium Cells in Tennessee. All five facilities operate as dual-purpose manufacturing hubs producing both ESS and EV batteries, providing the manufacturing flexibility needed to respond quickly to changing market demand.

This extensive manufacturing footprint is the result of a strategic rebalancing initiative that the company has pursued intensively over the past two and a half years. David Kim, CEO of LG Energy Solution, has outlined the strategy, stating, "We will actively pursue the rebalancing of our global production facilities to expand our business structure beyond EVs into ESS and new businesses, while optimizing production sites and maximizing the utilization of our investment assets." By rapidly adapting production capacity to shifting market conditions, the company has built one of the strongest manufacturing portfolios in the global battery industry.

LG Energy Solution is also building momentum in its EV battery business. LG Energy Solution recently announced the restart of EV cell production at the Ultium Cells facility in Ohio, which had temporarily paused operations earlier this year. Meanwhile, its Queen Creek facility in Arizona is expected to begin mass production of 46-series cylindrical batteries in the fourth quarter, supported by production lines with approximately 50 percent higher equipment efficiency compared with previous configurations.

Building on its strong manufacturing foundation, LG Energy Solution continues to secure new business opportunities. In the ESS sector, the company has signed agreements with major customers including Tesla, Terra-Gen, Excelsior Energy Capital, EG4, and Hanwha Qcells. In May, it signed an ESS battery supply agreement totaling 6GWh with DTE Energy. In July, the company also agreed to collaborate with renewable energy independent power producer Cypress Creek Energy on ESS supply for Google's largest solar-plus-storage project, with potential volumes reaching up to 2.9GWh. In the EV sector, LG Energy Solution continues to expand partnerships with global automakers, including Mercedes-Benz, while broadening its customer base for mid-priced battery products such as LFP and high-voltage mid-nickel batteries, particularly in Europe.

“The launch of the Lansing facility represents an important milestone that will accelerate the growth of LG Energy Solution’s North American business,” said Kim. “By establishing an advanced battery manufacturing network that supports the future of America’s mobility industry and energy infrastructure, we will continue strengthening the U.S. battery ecosystem while expanding our local production capabilities.”

title: CEA's BESS Mandate Could Accelerate Battery Makers' Shift Beyond EVs
description:
For battery manufacturers that built their businesses largely around electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers, four-wheelers and light commercial vehicles, the emerging stationary-storage market offers another major source of demand.
Beyond Electric Mobility The emerging BESS market is also allowing lithium-ion battery manufacturers to diversify beyond electric mobility.
Amara Raja Energy & Mobility told investors after its FY26 results that it was giving BESS a larger role in its mix.
“The industry keeps trying to sell a blended Rs /kWh tariff that folds battery costs into solar energy.
State-level rules also remain inconsistent, particularly around banking and surcharge provisions for commercial and industrial storage projects, Ezhil said.
text:
The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) has proposed making battery energy storage systems (BESS) mandatory for all new ground-mounted solar and onshore wind projects commissioned from 1 July 2027, a move that could accelerate the battery industry's shift beyond electric mobility into stationary storage.

Under the draft rules, a 100 MW solar or wind project would need at least 10 MW of storage capacity with a minimum two-hour duration. The requirement would rise to four hours for projects commissioned from July 2029.

The proposal comes as India's need for grid-scale storage is expected to expand sharply. The country added 2,668.54 MW of BESS power capacity, equivalent to 7,785.6 MWh of storage in 2026. Solar capacity stood at 164.59 GW and wind at 58.14 GW as of 31 July.

For battery manufacturers that built their businesses largely around electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers, four-wheelers and light commercial vehicles, the emerging stationary-storage market offers another major source of demand.

A Formalisation, Not A Surprise

The proposed mandate largely formalises a transition that is already visible in procurement. “Buyers have stopped asking for vanilla solar in the last few months — every serious conversation in the last months has been peak-power or solar-plus-storage,” said Sudharman Ezhil, Director & CEO, Natrinai Ventures (NGE Green Energy).

Ezhil said storage makes renewable assets more useful to lenders and offtakers by allowing projects to schedule power, manage deviation settlement and participate in evening demand periods, when time-of-day tariffs and exchange prices can be significantly higher than daytime solar rates. “What CEA has done is set a floor... it's a welcome move,” he said.

Ezhil expects storage to become standard within two to three years, irrespective of the mandate, as buyers look for projects that can provide power beyond solar generation hours. NGE Green, for instance, already treats BESS as a default line item. The system is sized according to the offtaker's load rather than the regulatory minimum.

Beyond Electric Mobility

The emerging BESS market is also allowing lithium-ion battery manufacturers to diversify beyond electric mobility. Pratik Kamdar, Co-founder & CEO, Neuron Energy, said BESS “has the potential to become a significant new market for Indian lithium-ion battery manufacturers”, pointing to India's projected requirement of more than 236 GWh of BESS by 2031-32.

“This creates an opportunity to diversify beyond electric mobility and participate in utility-scale as well as commercial and industrial storage applications,” Kamdar said.

The shift is also beginning to appear in manufacturers' strategies. Amara Raja Energy & Mobility told investors after its FY26 results that it was giving BESS a larger role in its mix. “A major change in our strategy is the introduction of BESS as a larger part of our mix. Earlier, we had largely focused on EVs,” the company's management said.

For manufacturers, the opportunity extends beyond cells and battery packs to areas such as battery management systems, thermal management and monitoring technologies.

Same Cells, Different Engineering

The move into stationary storage, however, is not a straightforward extension of EV battery manufacturing. “BESS cannot be treated as a simple extension of an EV battery platform,” Kamdar said, pointing to differences in operating requirements, including long-duration operation and frequent charge-discharge cycles.

“Battery pack architecture, BMS software, monitoring and thermal-management systems need to be designed around the specific operating profile of stationary storage,” Kamdar added.

At the same time, the underlying expertise developed through EV battery manufacturing remains transferable, giving existing lithium-ion manufacturers a starting point as they move into grid-scale and commercial storage.

Regulatory Gaps Persist

While the market opportunity is expanding, developers point to commercial and regulatory issues that could affect the pace of deployment.

Ezhil said one challenge is the way solar-plus-storage projects are priced. “The industry keeps trying to sell a blended Rs /kWh tariff that folds battery costs into solar energy. That structure fails bankability,” he said.

Ezhil argued that solar and storage need separate capacity and energy charges, or that batteries should be deployed behind the meter, to better reflect the different functions and costs of the two assets.

State-level rules also remain inconsistent, particularly around banking and surcharge provisions for commercial and industrial storage projects, Ezhil said.

Tamil Nadu's resource adequacy plan, for instance, projects a need for more than 11 GW of additional storage by 2035 and flags evening-hour power shortages between October and April. “The regulatory framework should be pulling private storage into that gap, and we are waiting eagerly for the new policy to get going,” Ezhil said.

The CEA has invited comments on its draft proposal until 4 October 2026, before the regulations are finalised.

For India's battery manufacturers, the proposed mandate could provide further impetus for stationary storage to develop from a supplementary market into a significant part of the country's power infrastructure.

name: Clean Energy
title: How China's manufacturing upgrade can expand global demand - CGTN
description:
The debate over China's manufacturing strength has moved beyond disputes over subsidies, market access and competition in individual industries.
China's industrial expansion may require adjustment in particular sectors, but the threat does not arise from trade.
In such industries, supply does not merely compete for existing demand; improvements in price and performance help create new demand.
Chinese exports therefore do not merely compete with existing production; many become inputs into production elsewhere.
A major contraction in Chinese demand would hurt many exporters precisely because China is one of their largest markets.
text:
Editor's note: Li Lun, a special commentator for CGTN, is an assistant professor of economics at Peking University. The article reflects the author's opinions and not necessarily the views of CGTN.

The debate over China's manufacturing strength has moved beyond disputes over subsidies, market access and competition in individual industries. As Chinese firms advance from labor-intensive exports into electric vehicles, batteries, solar equipment, industrial robots and other technology-intensive sectors, some foreign commentaries have turned those sectoral disputes into a broader warning about global stability. The claim is no longer merely that Chinese companies are intensifying competition for established producers, but that the world may be unable to absorb what China produces, potentially creating an imbalance that could trigger the next global economic crisis.

A recent article in Foreign Affairs by Michael Froman, former US trade representative and current president of the US think tank Council on Foreign Relations, takes this argument to its broadest conclusion. Froman contends that policy-directed credit, industrial subsidies and local government incentives have created manufacturing capacity beyond what either China's domestic market or the world economy can absorb. His proposed solution is a coordinated arrangement in the spirit of the Plaza Accord, the 1985 agreement among the US, UK, France, Japan and then West Germany to address massive global trade imbalances by devaluing the US dollar. Froman's solution would ask China to strengthen its currency, reduce industrial support and accept verifiable export limits, with trading partners easing their restrictions according to the scale of China's compliance.

Froman warns that an abrupt loss of foreign demand would destabilize China, yet recommends export restrictions and continued trade pressure. The contradiction is clear: Those measures would help create the very shock he predicts. China's industrial expansion may require adjustment in particular sectors, but the threat does not arise from trade. It arises when governments respond to competitive pressure with tariffs, closed markets and fragmented supply chains, thereby reducing the demand, investment and productivity on which global growth depends.

Froman presents his view as a matter of arithmetic, comparing a more than 20% increase in China's trade surplus in the first two months of 2026 with global economic growth of about 3%. But a trade surplus is not the same as exports. It is the gap between exports and imports, so it can widen without China's overseas sales growing at anything close to the same rate. The comparison assumes that world demand is fixed: If Chinese firms sell more, producers elsewhere must sell less. That assumption is particularly misleading in industries where falling costs and improving technology create new commercial applications and expand demand.

Consider solar power. When cheaper panels reduce the total cost of a power project, investments that were previously uneconomic can become viable, creating additional demand for installation, storage, grid equipment, financing and maintenance. Batteries follow the same pattern. Lower battery costs make electric vehicles more affordable, but they also enable grid storage, backup power for data centers, distributed power systems and other applications that were not commercially viable at earlier prices. In such industries, supply does not merely compete for existing demand; improvements in price and performance help create new demand.

This is also the logic behind China's manufacturing upgrade. Adjustment does not have to mean simply producing less until supply fits today's market. It can mean producing differently: improving technology, reducing costs, developing better products and making new applications commercially feasible.

In the first seven months of 2026, China's output of 3D-printing equipment, lithium-ion batteries and industrial robots rose by 52.3%, 40.2% and 28.5%, respectively. These products are not merely final goods competing for existing consumer spending. An affordable industrial robot can make automation viable for a smaller factory. Cheaper storage can support additional renewable generation, grid balancing and distributed power systems. Better batteries can stimulate investment in charging networks, power electronics, software and mobility services. Each technology creates demand for complementary capital, skills and services.

The economic dynamic extends beyond China. Lower-cost machinery, energy equipment and industrial components can reduce the capital required for factories, power systems and infrastructure in other countries. Affordable lithium iron phosphate batteries, for example, have helped electric vehicles move beyond the largest advanced economies and into a wider range of emerging markets. Importing a less expensive piece of equipment can enable a local firm to enter a market, expand production or adopt a technology that was previously out of reach. Chinese exports therefore do not merely compete with existing production; many become inputs into production elsewhere.

China also supports world demand from the other side of the trade ledger. In the first half of 2026, China's goods imports rose by 22.1%, faster than the 13.4% increase in exports. China buys commodities, intermediate goods, capital equipment, services and consumer products from around the world. A major contraction in Chinese demand would hurt many exporters precisely because China is one of their largest markets. Describing China only as a source of excess supply therefore misses half of the relationship: Its imports also sustain production and employment abroad.

These trade figures show why "overcapacity" cannot be inferred from exports or trade surpluses alone. A trade surplus is a macroeconomic outcome influenced by economy-wide saving and investment as well as international specialization, whereas excess capacity is an industry-level condition. Subsidies, low prices and strong exports may warrant scrutiny, but none is by itself decisive evidence of overcapacity.

Pressure on incumbent producers is also not proof that Chinese manufacturing reduces global welfare. A report by the Deutsche Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, shows that Chinese competition is only part of the explanation for Germany's export weakness: Weak demand for key German products, energy costs, supply-chain disruptions, an unfavorable export mix and broader competitiveness problems have also mattered. Treating Chinese output as the sole cause therefore shifts attention away from weaknesses that are partly domestic. Lower-priced imports can impose real pressure on established manufacturers while reducing costs for consumers and downstream businesses; a balanced assessment must account for both.

The more immediate global risk arises when governments try to prevent that evolution through trade restrictions. Restrictive trade policies intensified sharply in early 2026. In January-May, the World Trade Organization-International Monetary Fund measure of trade policy activity averaged nearly twice its 2024 level, with tariff increases, import bans and quantitative restrictions driving most of the rise. Such policies raise the cost of consumer goods and industrial inputs, force companies to duplicate factories across political blocs, weaken economies of scale and make businesses more reluctant to invest when future market access is uncertain.

A sudden worldwide closure to Chinese production is neither costless nor the most likely outcome. A joint venture between China's CATL, a global leader in renewable energy technology innovation, and automaker Stellantis in Spain is expected to create more than 4,000 direct jobs. Chinese new energy vehicle manufacturer BYD reported that its manufacturing complex in Brazil had produced 100,000 electrified vehicles and employed 5,500 direct workers by July 2026. Local production, joint ventures and supplier partnerships allow importing economies to capture more employment and value while continuing to benefit from Chinese technology. Market access is not a binary choice between unrestricted imports and complete exclusion.

text:
Apex Clean Energy has entered into a new power purchase agreement with Meta tied to the 144 MW Starling Solar project in Gonzales County, Texas, marking the seventh transaction between the companies and bringing their combined renewable energy portfolio to approximately 1,200 MW.

Under the agreement, Meta will receive exclusive rights to all environmental attributes associated with energy generated by Starling Solar, including the project’s renewable energy credits.

The project will add new solar generation to the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, or ERCOT, grid. Apex said the facility would not have been built without Meta’s commitment, highlighting the role large corporate energy buyers can play in supporting development of new generation capacity.

Starling is expected to begin commercial operations in 2027.

The project extends a relationship between Apex and Meta that now spans nearly seven years and includes projects across Texas, Virginia, Illinois, Kansas and Iowa.

With Starling, the companies’ combined portfolio reaches approximately 1.2 GW of renewable energy capacity.

The latest agreement comes as technology companies and other large electricity users seek new power resources to support growing energy requirements, including demand associated with data centers and AI infrastructure.

Apex positions its development strategy around identifying, interconnecting and preparing utility-scale projects that can be built on timelines compatible with the needs of large electricity consumers.

Starling represents another example of that strategy, pairing a ready-to-build Texas solar development with Meta’s long-term clean energy requirements.

The project is also expected to generate significant economic benefits in Gonzales County.

Apex estimates Starling Solar will produce approximately $27 million in tax revenue over its operating life.

Of that amount, approximately $15.6 million is expected to support local schools.

The project is also projected to generate more than $26.3 million in payments to participating landowners, creating a long-term source of income for property owners hosting project infrastructure.

Construction is expected to create approximately 400 to 450 jobs.

Apex also expects Starling to provide nearly $400,000 in grant funding for local organizations and conservation initiatives.

Those local economic benefits are an important component of the development model for large renewable energy projects, particularly in rural communities where utility-scale facilities can create new tax revenue and landowner income without requiring the same level of municipal services associated with other forms of development.

For Meta, the Starling agreement adds another renewable energy project to a broader strategy of supporting new generation in regions where the company operates and consumes electricity.

Rather than simply purchasing existing renewable attributes, the agreement supports a new project that Apex said represents additional generation capacity for the Texas grid.

Texas has become one of the country’s largest markets for new solar, wind, battery storage and other energy infrastructure, supported by substantial electricity demand and a relatively fast-growing power market.

Increasing demand from data centers, manufacturing facilities and population growth has further elevated the importance of adding generation capacity to ERCOT.

The Starling agreement illustrates how corporate power commitments can provide developers with the commercial certainty required to finance and construct new projects.

For Apex, the transaction further expands a major customer relationship while demonstrating its ability to repeatedly develop projects for one of the world’s largest technology companies.

The approximately 1,200 MW portfolio developed through the seven Meta transactions also provides geographic diversification across five states.

Apex develops, constructs and operates utility-scale wind, solar and energy storage projects, along with distributed energy resources, across the United States.

The company uses a data-focused development approach to identify projects capable of meeting the power, timing and sustainability requirements of large customers.

Starling Solar will now move toward construction and its planned 2027 commercial operation date, adding 144 MW of new capacity to the Texas grid while extending one of Apex’s longest-running corporate renewable energy relationships.

“Starling brings new capacity to Texas and lasting value to Gonzales County long after construction wraps.”

Ken Young, CEO of Apex Clean Energy

“The best clean energy projects are the ones the surrounding community feels the benefit of directly—in school funding, in landowner payments, in local hiring.”

“Starling brings all of that to Gonzales County, along with new solar generation for a Texas grid.”

Executive Summary

Over the past decade, governments in developed economies have expanded the use of public financing tools to support the development of clean energy and critical materials technologies. Instruments such as grants, concessional loans, guarantees, offtake arrangements, and tax credits have been deployed to address climate, energy, supply chain, and geopolitical objectives. As technologies evolve from early research through demonstration and then commercial scale, policy effectiveness changes depending on the instrument used. This task force report, which synthesizes insights from two expert roundtable discussions on the past decade of US industrial policy, highlights key lessons on how governments can sequence public finance tools as technologies and projects mature.

Key findings of this report include the following:

Technology development and deployment failures can stem not only from insufficient amounts of government support but also from the misapplication of instruments as technology risk profiles change. The same instrument can be effective at one technology readiness level (TRL) but less effective at another.

To ensure that policy tools are targeting the specific risk at hand—whether it be technical and scientific risk, execution and performance risk, or scale-up and commercial risk—governments need to recalibrate public support at each development stage.

For technologies at early stages of development (TRL 1–3), such as plasma separation for rare earth elements or direct internal recycling for nuclear fusion, distributing small and flexible grants across a large number of participants allows multiple technological pathways to be pursued simultaneously. Tolerating some level of “failure” across a portfolio of projects is a design requirement, not a weakness.

For technologies at middle stages of development (TRL 4–7), such as small modular reactors or superhot rock geothermal, cost-sharing agreements can outperform straight grants by enhancing incentive alignment and introducing outside commercial discipline. This stage requires industrial policy that addresses both the expensive and risky first-of-a-kind (FOAK) construction needs of TRL 4–7. Sliding-scale cost-share ratios reflect the risk level of the recipient, and milestone-based technical validation by public agencies can operate as a financing instrument by providing private capital with a credible signal of technical viability.

For projects at later stages of development (TRL 8–9), such as conventional mineral extraction and lithium iron phosphate battery manufacturing, revenue stabilization instruments are critical for securing the substantial project finance debt typically required for projects in this phase. Permitting and regulatory uncertainty can also become more binding constraints than residual technology risk at this stage.

Political durability of public programs that support the ability of technologies and projects to secure financing requires deliberate institutional design. Arm’s-length lending agencies, credible public narratives about acceptable failure rates, and multiyear program authorization can help industrial policy programs survive political cycles.
