In 2017, SAIC Motor and CATL established SAIC-CATL, and incorporated power battery production capacity directly into its own supply system through a joint venture.
After years of capacity expansion, the production capacity of power batteries has been greatly improved, and the industry is even facing overcapacity and price competition.
Power battery manufacturing is a typical large-scale manufacturing industry.
Its business also covers multiple fields such as power batteries, energy storage, lithium batteries and sodium batteries.
After incorporating cell manufacturing capabilities into its own industrial chain system, Leapmotor has realized 100% self-sufficiency in power battery production and manufacturing.
text:
If new energy vehicle manufacturers fail to master power battery technology, it is just like the era of traditional fuel vehicles when automakers could not get a grip on engine technology. What is thought-provoking is why few automakers poured money into developing engines in the past, while a large number of car companies are now eager to produce batteries.

Some time ago, two news related to power batteries in the new energy vehicle industry quietly gained traction:

First, Li Auto invested 2.65 billion yuan to participate in the capital increase and share expansion of Sunwoda Electric Vehicle Battery. After the capital increase, it will directly hold 8.79% of the shares of Sunwoda EVB. Combined with the old shares, Li Auto indirectly holds a total of 11.17% of the shares, becoming the second largest shareholder of Sunwoda EVB.

Second, Xiaomi launched its Dragon Armor Battery, with production tied to Sunwoda and CALB. Although it did not take a large equity stake, Xiaomi will take the lead in defining cell formulas, BMS and Pack solutions, while Sunwoda and CALB are responsible for OEM production.

Shifting from purchasing off-the-shelf cells to having automakers define cells, the apparent reason seems to be to reduce costs and improve efficiency. But beneath the surface, the fundamental driver is the intensifying involution in the new energy vehicle industry, as carmakers try to take back control of core components to secure their position in the market.

But is it really that easy for automakers to produce batteries on their own?

01

From the battery shortage era to the present, batteries have always been the core lifeline

If we go back to the early stage of the development of the new energy vehicle industry, the most direct anxiety of automakers about power batteries was actually "not being able to get high-quality batteries".

When the sales of new energy vehicles grew rapidly, the production capacity of power batteries was far less sufficient than it is today, and the prices of raw materials such as lithium, nickel and cobalt experienced drastic fluctuations, giving battery enterprises stronger bargaining power.

For automakers, batteries are not only one of the most core components of new energy vehicles, but also the link in the supply chain that most easily affects the delivery and cost of the whole vehicle.

Therefore, automakers began to reach out to the battery industry chain on a large scale for the first time. But the way of playing at that time was different from now. The 1.0 era of automakers producing batteries was more like "finding a battery factory for themselves".

The most typical example is the "Times" series of cooperation.

In 2017, SAIC Motor and CATL established SAIC-CATL, and incorporated power battery production capacity directly into its own supply system through a joint venture. Similar cooperation kept emerging, and automakers and battery enterprises bound production capacity and supply relations through joint ventures, equity participation and other methods.

Volkswagen took a similar path. In 2020, Volkswagen Group invested in Gotion High-Tech, planning to acquire 26.47% of Gotion High-Tech's shares through an investment of about 1.1 billion euros, becoming its largest shareholder.

For Volkswagen, which was accelerating its new energy transformation at that time, investing in a Chinese power battery enterprise was essentially to grasp an important link of the battery supply chain in its own hands.

In addition, new car-making forces are also looking for their own battery partners one after another. NIO has made a strategic investment in Welan New Energy, and the three companies of NIO, Li Auto and Xpeng have successively invested in Sunwoda...

At this stage, the idea of automakers is not complicated. They do not have to produce batteries by themselves, but cannot be completely controlled by others. Therefore, the core of the 1.0 era is to bind the supply chain.

No matter it is joint venture, equity participation, or establishing a battery company, the essence is to ensure stable battery supply and reduce dependence on a single supplier at the same time.

But a few years later, the contradiction of the industry has changed. The biggest trouble of power batteries today is no longer "whether there are good batteries available".

After years of capacity expansion, the production capacity of power batteries has been greatly improved, and the industry is even facing overcapacity and price competition. What really troubles automakers has become how to make batteries cheaper, safer and more efficient.

Power batteries have evolved from a supply chain issue to a mandatory question about vehicle cost and product competitiveness. It directly affects the range, fast charging performance, safety, space utilization and service life of vehicles, and is also the core component that accounts for a relatively high proportion of the cost of new energy vehicles.

In short, whether a new energy vehicle is affordable, charges fast, or has a long range is inseparable from power batteries behind the scenes.

As a result, the demands of automakers have changed for the second time, from "I need to ensure battery supply" to the current "I need to directly participate in deciding how this battery is made".

This is the starting point of the 2.0 era of automakers producing batteries.

02

There are still obstacles in the 2.0 era of automakers producing batteries

When it comes to automakers developing batteries on their own, BYD is almost impossible to avoid. Because in the current narrative of China's automotive industry, BYD has proved with practical results that if batteries are truly mastered in their own hands, they can become part of the competitiveness of the whole vehicle.

From Blade Battery, to cells and Packs, and then to materials and complete vehicles, BYD has long been engaged in vertical integration. At BYD, the battery is not an isolated business, but a system embedded in the R&D, manufacturing and supply chain system of the whole vehicle.

So now many automakers want to learn from BYD. But the real difficulty in making a battery is never to build a plant and move equipment into it; what people often see is only the battery factory, but rarely the things behind the factory.

The first threshold lies in the upstream industry.

If key raw materials such as lithium, cathode materials, anode materials and electrolyte still rely heavily on external procurement, then having its own cell factory does not mean that the automaker has truly mastered the battery cost. Once the price of raw materials rises, the cost pressure will still be transmitted downstream.

The second threshold is material and cell R&D.

Power batteries are not as simple as buying ready-made materials and assembling them. From material systems and formulas to powder modification, pole piece manufacturing and cell structure, every link will affect energy density, cycle life, safety and cost.

The third threshold is the manufacturing capacity that is most easily ignored.

Power battery manufacturing is a typical large-scale manufacturing industry. A difference of a few percentage points in yield rate, when applied to a production capacity of tens of GWh or even hundreds of GWh, will lead to a very large cost gap. Equipment operation rate, manufacturing rhythm, process consistency and quality control all require a lot of time to polish.

This is also the part of BYD that is really hard to replicate. BYD's advantage never lies in "having a battery factory", but in its interconnected systematic capabilities covering materials, cells, Packs, three electric systems and complete vehicles.

Battery R&D can support vehicle design, and vehicle sales can in turn dilute the R&D and manufacturing costs of batteries. The scale will further promote supply chain optimization, and finally form a positive cycle.

This is completely different from simply building a single battery factory.

There is no doubt that equating "producing batteries on our own" with "mastering battery capabilities" is a foolish act. Under this premise, the reason why Li Auto and Xiaomi are increasing investment and cooperating in depth with battery manufacturers is that they are making further explorations to test the boundary of automakers' battery manufacturing capabilities.

03

There is no shortage of battery production capacity, but high-quality GWh capacity is still scarce

Of course, on the road of automakers producing batteries, there are also players who have gone further. They either have strong backers as endorsement, or have strong sales to support their business.

For example, Geely is expanding its layout of battery business.

Information disclosed in 2026 shows that its Shield Golden Brick Battery has formed a production capacity reserve of 70~80GWh, and plans to reach 200GWh in 2027 and hit 300GWh in 2028. Its business also covers multiple fields such as power batteries, energy storage, lithium batteries and sodium batteries.

This scale is quite considerable across the whole industry.

Another example is Leapmotor, which has jointly built a cell production base with CALB.

The two sides previously announced an investment of 7.5 billion yuan to build an intelligent power battery manufacturing base with a planned production capacity of 33.6GWh. After incorporating cell manufacturing capabilities into its own industrial chain system, Leapmotor has realized 100% self-sufficiency in power battery production and manufacturing.

Hive Energy is another well-known example.

Great Wall Motors spun off its internally incubated battery business into Hive Energy in 2018, with the group holding the shares and supplying products to the external market. In 2019, Hive Energy set up a joint venture factory with Sinowatt, and in 2020 it introduced strategic investment from SDIC Venture Capital, becoming a typical example of "internally generated" power battery business from automakers.

Looking at these cases together, the change is very obvious — what automakers really want to take back is the right to define batteries, including:

First, the underlying right to define cells: finalize the chemical system, size, packaging and material formula of cells, get rid of the off-the-shelf products on battery manufacturers' shelves, and customize cells around the vehicle platform.

Second, the right to define vehicle integration: take the lead in the CTP/CTC/CTB integrated structure, cooling, sealing and body integration solutions, so that the battery becomes a structural part of the vehicle, rather than an independent component.

Third, the right to define BMS and thermal management algorithms: master the underlying algorithms such as SOC estimation, charging and discharging strategies, thermal runaway protection and aging models, and get rid of the black box solutions from suppliers.

Fourth, the right to define supply chain and cost: independently select upstream materials and plan production capacity to hedge against raw material price fluctuations, and control the cost structure and supply rhythm.

Fifth, the right to define safety standards: on the basis of national standards, independently develop test specifications for cells and battery packs to define the safety boundary of batteries.

Sixth, the right to define the rhythm of technology iteration: the battery R&D cycle matches the launch rhythm of new vehicles, and independently decides the launch timing of new battery systems.

Seventh, the right to define multi-scenario reuse: one set of battery technology can be adapted to passenger vehicles, energy storage and other scenarios at the same time, to dilute the fixed investment in R&D and production lines.

What is really scarce in the power battery market is never the number of GWh, but the GWh capacity that can achieve stable production, high yield rate, low cost and reliable quality.

From the perspective of automakers, only by mastering the right to define power batteries can they efficiently mobilize internal resources in the fiercely competitive market, win tough battles, and obtain more benefits at the same time.

Therefore, rather than saying that all automakers are learning from BYD to make batteries, it is better to say that they are all trying to stop the visible "blood loss points".

BYD's answer is to cover the whole industrial chain. Other automakers do not necessarily need to fully replicate this path.

However, in terms of power battery layout, if they only learn to "build a battery factory" without the capabilities of material R&D, supply chain management, manufacturing yield improvement and vehicle coordination, in the end they are likely to only turn the past supply chain pressure into their own asset pressure, which is not worth the loss!

title: At Glen Canyon Dam, Trump administration privileges hydropower over ecosystems | KUNC
authors: Brett Walton, Circle of Blue, www.kunc.org

text:
In the struggling Colorado River basin, where water is scarce, the White House has signaled its priorities for how to use the remaining gallons.

Even as scientifically-determined thresholds have been met for releasing water from Glen Canyon Dam for ecological and recreational benefits in Grand Canyon, the Trump administration has decided against those actions in this record-hot year – deciding not to release cold water from deep in Lake Powell to aid the humpback chub, a threatened fish species, and not to authorize a high-volume release of water to rebuild Grand Canyon’s eroded beaches, which are in terrible condition, according to federal monitoring.

These environmental releases would not change the total volume of water flowing out of Lake Powell over the year, just the timing.

Because the releases bypass the dam’s turbines and reduce hydropower generation, which is part of the administration’s “energy dominance” agenda, the Bureau of Reclamation, the federal agency that manages Glen Canyon Dam, will not be doing them.

“After evaluating management alternatives and considering all authorized purposes, the decision was made based on significant hydropower generation concerns under already strained system conditions,” Reclamation said in a statement in August.

The administration’s decisions foreshadow more difficult choices ahead. Due to climate change and overuse, the Colorado River is shrinking and warming. Its dams were built and river management goals were laid out during an era that anticipated healthy reservoirs. That is no longer the case. Because Lake Powell and Lake Mead are about a quarter of their capacity or less, the hydrological assumptions that inform current management strategies are outdated, said Jack Schmidt, a scientist who has spent his four-decade career studying the Colorado River.

“Everything needs to be revisited because the driving factors of the Colorado River ecosystem in Grand Canyon are now completely changed and probably forever changed,” said Schmidt of Utah State University’s Center for Colorado River Studies. “Everything was developed in a world of full reservoirs. And now the reservoirs are empty.”

Tradeoffs plague water managers

Even in the best of times, managing a large dam on a major river is not easy. Dams alter the river’s natural patterns of flow and temperature. Operators must weigh one set of benefits against another group of costs.

Glen Canyon Dam is one of the thorniest management conundrums. Located near the Arizona-Utah border, the 63-year-old structure has emerged as themost significant water-supply choke point in the Colorado River basin and it is the focus of clamorous debate about water and power infrastructure in a drier climate.

As managers grapple with how much water to release, Glen Canyon Dam is also choking the river of its natural supply of sediment. Without new inputs, sand bars and beaches in Grand Canyon are at risk of disappearing. These features provide habitat, give boaters a place to camp during river trips, and protect archaeological sites.

Most of the river’s sediment now comes from the Paria River and Little Colorado River, downstream of Glen Canyon. Periodic high-flow water releases from the dam mimic the thunderous floods of the past that carried sediment through Grand Canyon to fortify eroding beaches.

There is enough sediment in the Colorado River below Glen Canyon today to warrant a high-flow release. Yet Reclamation has not done one since 2023. Experts agree that Reclamation is highly unlikely to conduct one this fall either. A final decision will be made in the next few weeks.

The need for a high-flow release is mounting. In August, David Topping, a research hydrologist at the U.S. Geological Survey’s Grand Canyon Monitoring and Research Center,presented data showing the ill health of Grand Canyon beaches. A typical sand bar is smaller now than in 2016, when the current management plan that established the high-flow triggers was finalized.

The lack of high-flow releases has deprived researchers of crucial data on how the size and duration of these mini-floods, usually one to four days in length, aid beach-building.

“What can we do if the administration isn’t willing to allow us to use the bypass tubes for high-flow experiments, if that’s going to be off the table, at least for a while?” said Wayne Pullan, Reclamation’s Upper Colorado Region director, at a Glen Canyon management meeting in August, asking attendees to consider management options under political constraints.

“We’re in a pinch point,” Pullan added. “A real pinch point.”

Degraded beaches result in a degraded river experience, said David Brown of the Grand Canyon River Guides, a recreation advocacy group. Rafting groups have to compete for limited real estate in what is generally regarded as one of the world’s premier river corridors.

“When there's less campable area, that means everyone's kind of getting squished together or your toilet is next to where people are sleeping,” Brown said.

Non-native species thrive in warm water

In addition to sediment, water temperature is the other blinking red environmental indicator.

Air temperature records in the basin are being obliterated this year. Colorado, home to the river’s headwaters, had its hottest summer ever. Scorching air temperatures are reflected in water. The Colorado River below Lake Powell is the warmest since Glen Canyon Dam was completed.

Smallmouth bass were introduced as a sport fish in the upper Colorado River basin in the late 1960s. Voracious feeders, smallmouth bass view other fish as the sport, happily preying on threatened native species like the humpback chub, an eighteen-inch fish in Grand Canyon with a distinctive smooshed silhouette.

Listed as endangered in 1967, the humpback chub has now bounced back thanks to tens of millions of dollars of conservation investment. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service upgraded the humpback chub to “threatened” status in 2018.

Smallmouth bass live in Lake Powell, preferring the layer of warm water closest to the surface. As the lake shrinks, that warm layer has now reached the level of the penstocks, which pull water into Glen Canyon Dam’s turbines for hydropower generation before being released downstream.

In these low-water conditions, the fear is that more smallmouth bass will be delivered into the Colorado River below Glen Canyon.

Once there, they will find a habitable environment. Smallmouth bass spawn when water temperatures exceed 60 degrees Fahrenheit. This year, that mark was breached in June. Today, the river at Lees Ferry, about 16 miles downstream of Glen Canyon Dam, is about 70 F.

These conditions – when the river temperature is above 60 F for three consecutive days – are supposed to trigger a release of cold water from deep in Lake Powell. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Servicesays that this “cool mix” is the “only conservation measure proven to limit smallmouth bass reproduction.” Evidence from cool mix releases in 2024 and 2025, which knocked down smallmouth bass numbers, supports that conclusion.

Cool mix, however, will not happen in 2026 due to the Trump administration’s desire to generate hydropower.

The last cool mix flow, in 2025, cost the Western Area Power Administration, which markets federal hydropower, $6.1 million to replace that electricity for its contractors.

Instead of cool mix, Reclamation says it is focusing on other options to keep smallmouth bass from establishing downstream of Glen Canyon and to preserve the humpback chub’s hard-won conservation gains. In the short term that means stunning the bass with electric-shock tools and physically removing them from the water.

In the longer term, Reclamation is considering installing infrastructure to regulate the temperature of the water that passes through Glen Canyon. The agency calls this one of its “durable structural solutions.”

An uncertain future

Cool mix and high-flow releases are an attempt to rebalance an ecosystem that the dams destabilized. Congress passed the Grand Canyon Protection Act of 1992, which orders Reclamation to operate Glen Canyon Dam in a manner that protects and reduces harm to the “natural and cultural resources and visitor use.” That is, fish, tribal archaeological sites, and rafting.

The act required an environmental impact statement for Glen Canyon Dam that would analyze the actions required to achieve the broad environmental-protection goals set by Congress.

It was a “compromise to really put all the resources on the same playing field,” said Jen Pelz of the Grand Canyon Trust. In her view, decisions this year tilt in one direction – hydropower. “I don't feel like they're being balanced right now.”

Because the river guides were instrumental in lobbying for Grand Canyon protections, the present-day failures to uphold the act’s goals are all the more galling, Brown said. “It's very hard to watch it get ignored.”

The administration is prioritizing hydropower when hydropower is at a pivot point.

Generation at Glen Canyon is down more than 40% from when Lake Powell was full. Utilities are turning to solar and wind to cover some of the generation losses, while utility-scale batteries are helping to replace the capacity and grid-regulating functions that a large dam provides.

The decision to favor hydropower over ecology reflects bigger problems with the Colorado River’s infrastructure. Glen Canyon Dam is not designed for the river as it exists today. Reclamation wants to keep Lake Powell high enough to generate hydropower because the dam’s other outlets to deliver water downstream are untested over long periods and were damaged in a previous high-flow release.

Lower basin states and tribes, including Arizona, California, Nevada, and the Gila River Indian Community, have asked the federal government to update Glen Canyon’s infrastructure for water delivery and power generation. Reclamation is assessing three options and expects that study to be released in early 2027. Any additional action will require congressional approval and funding.

Along with the infrastructure problems, man-made climate change is sapping the river and heating up its water. Ecologists consider the Grand Canyon a “novel ecosystem,” meaning its native species and natural processes have been disrupted and rearranged by human meddling.

To Schmidt, the former chief of the U.S. Geological Survey’s Grand Canyon Monitoring and Research Center, this suggests a wholesale rethinking not just of the river’s infrastructure but also of our ecological goals for the Colorado River.

“We as a society get to play God in deciding what attributes of that ecosystem we value, which ones we want to work hard to preserve and which ones we don't,” he said. “The answer is not an obvious one.”

This story was produced by Circle of Blue, in partnership with The Water Desk at the University of Colorado Boulder’s Center for Environmental Journalism.

text:
SPRINGFIELD, Ill. (CAPITOL NEWS ILLINOIS) — Illinois has made substantial progress in reducing greenhouse gas emissions in recent years, but it is not yet on track to meet its goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2050.

That’s the conclusion of a new Comprehensive Climate Action Plan released this month by the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency.

To reach that goal, the report suggests Illinois will need to enact significant changes across virtually every sector of its economy, including transportation, building construction, manufacturing, agriculture and waste disposal.

“Illinoisans are seeing the extreme heat and storms climate change has brought to our doorstep this summer,” Illinois Climate Advisor JC Kibbey said in a statement announcing the report. “We are feeling the high, unpredictable costs of fossil fuel every time we reach for our wallets. This plan shows the great progress we’ve made on climate and clean energy — and how much more we have left to do.”

In 2024, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency awarded Illinois a $430 million grant to implement programs to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. That money came through the federal Climate Pollution Reduction Grant program, which was an element of then-President Joe Biden’s signature Inflation Reduction Act.

The Comprehensive Climate Action Plan is intended to provide a roadmap for Illinois to reduce its carbon footprint to as little as 72% below its 2005 baseline. It also outlines two scenarios under which Illinois could virtually eliminate all carbon emissions.

Those would involve a combination of incentive packages and regulatory changes that would affect nearly every sector of the economy. But doing so, the report suggests, would produce $21 billion a year in net economic benefits.

Current policies

According to the document, Illinois cut its net greenhouse gas emissions by 32% from 2005 to 2023. That was due mainly to a shift in electric generation toward natural gas and renewable sources such as wind and solar power.

The transportation industry also saw significant reductions due to improved fuel efficiency standards and the gradual adoption of electric vehicles.

Those trends are expected to continue into the future as long, the report states, as Illinois adheres to its current policies such as the 2021 Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, which calls for the complete elimination of carbon-emitting power production by 2050, and the state’s Electric Vehicle Rebate Program, which offers incentives for lower-income consumers to switch to electric vehicles.

But they will not be enough to reach the goal of net-zero emissions by 2050, according to the report. At best, without any additional policy changes, the report estimates net carbon emissions will only fall to 133 million metric tons by 2050, a 53% reduction below the 2005 baseline.

Path to further reductions

The document outlines a laundry list of additional actions Illinois could take to reduce its carbon footprint even further, starting with providing rebates and other incentives to convert all forms of commercial vehicles, including medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, to electric.

It also proposes new regulations on residential and commercial buildings. Those include adopting clean heat standards that would require a 22% reduction in emissions from natural gas by 2035, offering subsidies to install heat pumps in residential homes, adopting all-electric construction codes for new construction and phasing out gasoline-powered lawn and landscaping equipment by 2035.

It also proposes additional regulations for industrial activities such as requiring net zero emissions from cement production by 2050 and requiring reductions in emissions intensity of cement, glass, iron and steel used in public construction.

The plan also proposes stronger methane monitoring and abatement regulations for landfills and additional incentives for farmers to adopt practices that reduce carbon dioxide emissions.

The report estimates that adopting all the measures outlined in the plan would reduce the state’s carbon footprint to 79 million metric tons, or 72% below 2024 levels.

The document also outlines two scenarios for achieving a complete “net zero” footprint by 2050, both requiring high levels of energy efficiency and replacing fossil fuels with electrification or other kinds of renewable fuels.

One plan, called the “moderate efficiency and flexibility” scenario, assumes full electrification of buildings by 2050 with 32% of households using hybrid heat pumps. It also assumes a rapid expansion of electric vehicles.

The “high efficiency and flexibility” scenario places greater emphasis on reducing energy demand. It calls for shifting the focus of new residential development to multifamily buildings instead of single-family homes to reduce heating and cooling loads. It also calls for higher density development and increased reliance on public transportation to reduce the overall number of vehicle miles traveled on roads.

Costs and benefits

The report acknowledges that adopting the policies it outlines would require substantial new investments from the state, private industry and consumers. Those include costs for new infrastructure, vehicles, heat pumps and alternative fuels, to name a few.

But the report says those investments will also yield long-term cost savings from reduced fossil fuel consumption, greater efficiencies, reduced greenhouse gas emissions and improved health and air quality benefits.

It estimates the improvements in air quality alone would lead to between 392 and 631 fewer premature deaths per year. That translates to between $8.8 and $13.8 billion in avoided healthcare costs and increased worker productivity.

“Including the monetized benefits of reduced (greenhouse gas) emissions and health benefits, the total annual net benefit of the Increased State Action scenario reaches $21 billion by 2050,” the report concludes.

“Since adoption of the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, Illinois has been a national leader in addressing carbon emissions, particularly from the energy and transportation sectors,” Illinois EPA Director James Jennings said in a statement. “The (Comprehensive Climate Action Plan) builds on these past successes by identifying a path for Illinois to achieve significant reductions in climate change-causing greenhouse gases and meet the state’s long term climate goals.”

Global law firm Norton Rose Fulbright represented PowerTransitions, an independent power producer focused on redeveloping legacy facilities, in its acquisition and related financing of the Roseton Generating Facility in Newburgh, New York, from a subsidiary of Castleton Commodities International. The Roseton Generating Facility is a dual-fuel, natural gas-fired power plant with a 1,242 MW capacity that has supplied electricity since 1974. The facility's scale and grid infrastructure make it well-positioned for redevelopment into a multi-use energy campus, including new energy storage systems that could further support reliability in the region.

“This deal builds on the company’s recent New York investments and positions it to capitalize on growing demand for power and energy infrastructure across the region,” said Douglas Fried, who co-led Norton Rose Fulbright’s representation.

Norton Rose Fulbright also represented Partners Group and PowerTransitions in the acquisition of a portfolio of five power plants and related pipeline infrastructure serving multiple counties in New York which closed in July. name: Clean Energy
title: Iowa needs more power, not uncertainty on security reviews | Opinion
description:
In rural Iowa, land is never just land.
That is something people often misunderstand about rural Iowa.
For rural Iowa, this is about more than economic statistics.
It also means accepting that preserving rural Iowa does not mean freezing it in time.
We should modernize the infrastructure already standing, responsibly build what comes next, and establish clear rules that respect national security, private property, and local communities.
text:
Waylon Brown is a former Iowa state senator and a fourth-generation farmer from northern Iowa. He is senior policy director for the Clean Grid Alliance, an advocacy group.

In rural Iowa, land is never just land.

It is where your grandfather taught your father to straighten a fence post. It is where you learned to drive a tractor before you were old enough to drive a car. It is the field you check after a hard rain, the ground you worry about during a dry summer, and the farm you hope will still be in the family long after you are gone.

Every acre has a story. Every farm carries the work, sacrifice, and faith of the generations that came before.

As a fourth-generation farmer, I understand that connection because I live it. My family has worked the same ground through good years and bad ones. We have hosted wind turbines since the early 1990s and farmed alongside transmission infrastructure for decades. We understand both the responsibility of caring for the land and the importance of allowing it to provide new opportunities for the next generation.

That is something people often misunderstand about rural Iowa.

We are not afraid of change. We are afraid of losing control over the things generations of our families worked to preserve. We do not oppose progress. We simply want progress to respect the land, honor private property rights, and leave our communities stronger than it found them.

Today, Iowa faces a challenge that will help determine whether those communities grow or slowly disappear.

We need more electricity.

Manufacturers are expanding. Farms and rural businesses rely on more technology every year. New industries are searching for communities where they can invest and grow. The demand for electricity is rising, and the states capable of meeting that demand will win the jobs and opportunities of the future.

For rural Iowa, this is about more than economic statistics. It is about whether there will be enough opportunity for our children to come home.

It is about whether the school can keep its doors open, whether the volunteer fire department can replace an aging truck, whether the local hardware store still has customers, and whether a young family can build a life in the same community where their grandparents did.

Energy investment can help make that possible.

My family has seen firsthand what wind development can mean. It can provide steady income that helps a farm survive difficult years. It can generate tax revenue for schools, roads, emergency services, and other local needs. It can create work for contractors and bring economic activity to towns that rarely receive a second look from major investors.

All while farmers continue planting corn and soybeans and raising livestock on nearly all the ground surrounding the turbines.

Iowa has already built some of the strongest wind infrastructure in the country. Now we have an opportunity to get even more value from it by repowering older projects.

During my time in the Iowa Senate, I worked on issues involving wind repowering. Repowering replaces aging equipment with newer, more efficient technology. It allows an existing site to produce more electricity, protects landowner payments, preserves local tax revenue, and extends the life of an investment a community has already made room for.

That should be common sense.

But no farmer, business, or energy company can make a major investment without certainty.

A farmer does not buy seed without knowing how many acres will be planted. A small business does not hire workers without knowing whether it can make payroll. A family does not build a home without knowing whether it can obtain a permit.

Energy projects are no different.

Developers need to understand the rules and timelines. Landowners need to know what they can plan around. Counties need to know whether future tax revenue will be there. Local workers need to know whether the jobs they were promised will materialize.

When the rules suddenly change or government simply stops making decisions, uncertainty spreads far beyond a project’s balance sheet. It reaches the farmer counting on a lease payment, the county planning its next budget, and the community hoping an investment might give its young people another reason to stay.

That is why the recent federal uncertainty surrounding Department of Defense reviews of wind projects is so concerning.

National security must always come first. Wind projects should be carefully reviewed for potential effects on military radar, aviation, training, and readiness. Those concerns are legitimate and must be treated seriously.

But a serious review should produce an answer.

If a project creates a genuine national security concern, identify the problem and determine whether it can be addressed. If it does not, allow the project to move forward. Indefinite delays and unclear standards are not responsible government. They place rural families and communities in limbo while our country is calling for more domestic energy production.

The people who live on this land deserve better than uncertainty handed down from a distant office.

Understanding the land means understanding that decisions made today will outlive the people making them. It means recognizing that private property is not simply an asset on a spreadsheet. It is a family’s history and, if we are careful, its future.

It also means accepting that preserving rural Iowa does not mean freezing it in time.

Our parents and grandparents adopted electricity, tractors, combines, conservation practices, and technologies that transformed agriculture. They did not abandon their way of life. They adapted so that way of life could survive.

Our generation faces the same responsibility.

Iowa needs more power. We should modernize the infrastructure already standing, responsibly build what comes next, and establish clear rules that respect national security, private property, and local communities.

Because the real question is not whether rural Iowa will change. It always has.

The question is whether we will shape that change in a way that gives the next generation a reason to stay, a chance to succeed, and a place they will still be proud to call home.

Waylon Brown is a former Iowa state senator and a fourth-generation farmer from northern Iowa. He is senior policy director for the Clean Grid Alliance, an advocacy group.

text:
This week we’re passing the mic again to political organizer and climate policy specialist Alex Cool-Fergus.

This post appeared in Alex’s Climate Memes newsletter before the second of two science reports showing climate change spiralling out of control, before the Canadian Climate Institute warned that Canada is 20 years behind its 2030 emissions reduction target—and before the dealbook for PM Mark Carney’s Canada Investment Summit profiled several carbon capture and storage projects.

Alex’s case against carbon capture tech attached to oil and gas infrastructure is one more reason to double down on the renewable energy, energy storage, energy efficiency, and heat pump alternatives that we know we can count on—because we already do. After reading her post, you’ll also know why she calls her newsletter Climate Memes. You can subscribe here.

It’s finally here, the moment we’ve all feared since the Paris Agreement was struck with the laudable goal of achieving a “safe” level of 1.5° of warming: the UN acknowledged, in a report last week, that the world is on track to exceed 1.5° of warming over the coming years. If not permanently, then at least for most of my lifetime, and my kids’.

To be clear, while this is devastating and alarming, it is not the end of the fight. Every tenth of a degree means lives saved. Period. But we’ve collectively got to be a lot smarter about the design and implementation of climate policies if we want to avoid the very worst warming scenarios.

I thought this would be a good time to get back to the basis of climate policy. Over the past few years, the Canadian political and pundit class has mostly been debating the politics of climate policies, which is, essentially, their job. However, there have been some fairly appalling intellectual shortcuts, lack of understanding of basic physics (no, sadly, there is no carbon capture in the world that can actually decarbonize a barrel of oil), and punting the issue of addressing Canada’s increasing pollution from oil and gas to an unspecified date in the future when it will be someone else’s problem to deal with.

Given we can all agree that Mean Girls is an iconic piece of our shared cultural heritage, I thought it might help smooth over some of our deep anxieties about these issues. Enjoy.

Net Zero is So Fetch

Think forward to 2050. How old will you be? I’ll be in my 50s.

My sons will be the age I am now, which seems as implausible as the concept of decarbonized oil.

Net zero by 2050 is a bit like apple pie: nobody is ever against it. Everyone thinks it will happen, somehow, though the details are murky. When pollsters ask variations on the theme, “Do you agree that Canada/ Alberta/ the world/ oil and gas should achieve net zero by 2050?”, people overwhelmingly agree.The oil and gas engineers or boosters in my network all include some kind of “working towards net zero by 2050” in their Linkedin bios and social media handles. It’s so fetch! [I’ll freely admit that I needed to look it up, so for anyone else who was wondering—Ed.]

Thing is, unless we start working to net zero today, we have no chance of achieving it by 2050. Canada has officially committed to achieving net zero. That commitment was formalized in 2021 in the Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act (CNZEAA), a piece of legislation that not only sets the 2050 target, but also lays out the broad steps the federal government must take to meet that milestone. This is reasonable! It would be incredibly hard for the federal government to maintain a high-carbon status quo for the interim decades, and then turn the decarbonization dial up to max in the couple of years leading up to 2050.

But the step-by-step version of decarbonization appears to be too much for PM Mark Carney’s administration. So much so that a group of young people is taking the federal government to court over its refusal to implement measures in the Act—an action which the feds are asking the courts to strike down.

Classy.

Again, think of what you’ll be doing (or your chances of being alive, no offence) in and around 2050. Decarbonizing with no plan at a very fast pace over five or even 10 years would be near catastrophic for workers, public finances, industries, and entire communities. Think about it: emissions in Canada dropped by 7-9% in 2020, due to the enormous impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic. Much of the economy shut down for months, and hundreds of thousands of people lost their jobs. And emissions still only went down by between seven and nine percent. Nobody wants a repeat of that type of scenario.

Canada has so far appeared to reduce its emissions somewhat, but we are off track from where we are supposed to be by now. Most sectors of the economy—transportation, industry (non-oil and gas), buildings, and electricity—have made a dent in their own emissions. This is no accident: it is the result of long-term financial forecasting, technological shifts, and common sense—if everyone but your company moves towards electrification, you’ll risk being stuck with stranded assets which decrease your competitiveness.

So how quickly do we need to get those pesky emissions down? Well, the legion of scientists who contribute to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) say the best way to do it is by frontloading the low-hanging fruit of emissions cuts now, so that we can avoid the worst consequences of climate change in the 25 years we have between us and the net-zero world we and hundreds of other countries have committed to creating in 2050.

For reference, here’s what the IPCC says about the urgency of frontloading emissions reductions:

Avoiding overshoot and reliance on future large-scale deployment of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) can only be achieved if global CO2 emissions start to decline well before 2030.

Time to go, Glen Coco.

Every Five Years, We Set Interim Targets

Like any goal-setting exercise, the federal government is (or, at least until very recently, was) setting interim targets, and updating its roadmap to achieve them. Sen. Rosa Galvez produced a really helpful graph illustrating the legislative requirements the federal government set out for itself a few years ago.

Target-setting is a challenging balancing act which requires tonnes of data, as well as an eye to where the puck is going on decarbonization costs, technologies, and political and social feasibility. The feds haven’t always got it right (in fact, they haven’t ever hit a target), but since the first Emissions Reduction Plan was published in 2022, we’ve started to see a bend in Canada’s overall emissions, which was a positive start.

Until it wasn’t.

In recent years (okay, the past two), emissions in Canada have flatlined. Why? The removal of the controversial consumer-facing carbon price, as well as the end of successful programs such as the electric vehicle subsidy and Greener Homes grants, definitely didn’t help. But the biggest culprit is the oil industry, which, in addition to doing very little (read: nothing) to reduce its emissions, has been enjoying great years of high output. Canadian oil production has never been higher (boosted by increased export capacity and facility upgrades).

And now we’re all on the hook to build out even more oil and gas infrastructure. That’s not how you join the Mathletes, nerds.

Carbon Capture Will Decarbonize Everything. Right?

Carbon capture is like going on a diet, but increasing your overall calorie intake, only swapping out your accompanying Coke with a Diet Coke. At the end of the day, yeah, you’re ingesting fewer calories per Coke, but you’re still eating more than you should if you want to shed those three pounds for the Spring Fling.

Carbon capture sucks (but not enough to suck enough CO2 out of the air hehehe), and is not a fiscally responsible way to reduce emissions from oil and gas. But don’t take my word for it: here are some takes from folks further to the right of the political spectrum, with various forms of expertise.

• Former Energy Minister Joe Oliver thinks CCS is a fugly scam.

• Jason Kenney, former federal minister and Premier of Alberta, cast doubt on the competitiveness of oil paired with carbon capture and storage (a cruel irony, since the Harper government was such a CCS booster back in the day).

• Even the Fraser Institute which, to be clear, I do not condone as a serious source on anything, says: “Major infrastructure projects like this offer potential but will be difficult, costly, and resource intensive to implement.”

So that was the punditry. The actual facts look like this:

Carbon capture and storage in Canada currently counts for a -0.5% reduction in emissions. It cannot currently work at scale to reduce emissions from the oil and gas industry, and is not expected to achieve those enormous reductions anytime soon. The CCS project the Oilsands Alliance has been promoting for years (without putting its members’ own, significant funds, towards it) is opposed by the Cold Lake First Nation and tonnes of other residents along its route.

Carbon capture pipelines have been known to explode, creating horrific consequences for communities along the route. It is very expensive compared to a tonne of other measures, including limiting methane controls, industrial carbon pricing, or simply cutting the emissions in the first place by investing in cheaper energy options like solar, wind, and battery storage.

And at the end of the day, carbon capture and storage would only ever reduce the very small portion of emissions associated with oil production, not use—about 20% of the emissions in every barrel. So the term “decarbonized oil” is, at best, misleading. At worst, it would be a hugely expensive marketing scam diverting attention and funding for the very real energy transition that should be happening in Canada.

Nobody Wants ‘Decarbonized Oil’, Let’s Be Real Here

Yeah, so carbon capture and storage will not bring all the buyers to the yard. EVEN IF decarbonization were possible for 100% of the upstream emissions produced by a barrel of oil (to be clear, this is not feasible and never will be), the price of the decarbonization would make the production of said oil completely uncompetitive. And also, nobody is buying our spin.

Let’s check and see which countries are looking for “decarbonized” oil at the moment:

…

Ok. Moving on.

But, But, Doesn’t Oil Fuel Our Economy and Contribute Much-Needed Dollars to the Public Purse?!

Well, not really. Not when you consider how much runaway climate change costs Canadians, not to mention everyone else. I’m not going to mention the flooding in Nepal, because it’s just too damn obvious. If you were on vacation while it was happening, take a deep breath before looking up footage.

Back to the economy: oil and gas contributes 1/20th of Canada’s GDP. It’s at about 3.8%. Not nothing, but to put things into context, the non-profit sector contributes 8% of Canada’s GDP. And yet you don’t see people driving around with cringe “I love Canadian nonprofits” stickers on their cars.

Climate change is estimated to already be costing Canadians hundreds of dollars a year in lost revenue, in adaptation, increased insurance costs, health care, and much more. Are we really willing to invest further in the industries that have not been reducing their emissions, and continue to lay our cherished landscapes, not to mention our health and well-being, to waste?

New jobs in the energy transition could quickly outpace jobs in the fossil fuel industry, which are declining sharply as industry automates and moves away from new, labour-intensive projects.

Basically, oil and gas jobs soon won’t even go here.

Peak Oil is Coming (Like, Totes)

Demand for oil is expected to peak this decade due to a combination of factors, especially electrification in the markets that oil majors in Canada want to sell to. Now, I’ll acknowledge there is some controversy about this statement, after Trump’s administration leaned so heavily on the IEA to not repeat what they said in 2024. In 2025 the IEA essentially shrugged and said oil “could” continue to grow till 2050, in the same way I say my kids “could” not ever brush their teeth again and replace them with jelly beans. Either way, furthering our national economy’s overreliance on fossil fuels, especially oil, would be a mistake in the mid term, if not sooner.

Canadians pride ourselves on being un-American, but we rarely look beyond North America to see what the rest of the world is doing. If we did, we might notice that most advanced economies, and many emerging ones, are growing their renewable energy industries at a very rapid pace. (So rapid, in fact, that the government of Pakistan cancelled LNG imports from Qatar, due to the rapid deployment of solar panels which meet Pakistanis’ energy needs.)

So. Why does all this yapping about 2050 targets and oil matter, anyway?

Well, mostly because it shows that Canada is increasingly setting itself up to be stuck with a bunch of stranded assets, in a world moving to electrification and net zero. We continue to belch out millions of tonnes of emissions, putting our communities and the rest of the world’s at risk. It’s expensive, and dangerous. Read the UN report if you want to learn just how bad.

Where does that leave us? Frankly, not in a great position. The feds will continue to dismantle whatever is left of essential climate policies (especially now that the provinces and industry have understood that if they whine hard enough, they’ll get what they want). The oil and gas majors are the biggest beneficiaries here. They are likely to get new pipelines and LNG terminals, carbon capture and storage investment tax credits that they can use for enhanced oil recovery, as well as the removal of irksome policies that prevented them from doing whatever they want.

It’s not too late to turn the ship and become climate leaders, rather than laggards. But we must act very quickly to embrace a reasonable energy transition, rather than scramble once the rest of the world gets there first.

Basically, at the end of the day, listen to Coach Carr. Don’t build new oil infrastructure. If you do, you won’t hit net zero, and your economy will be stuck with stranded assets. Not fetch at all.

text:
Rune wants unused solar electricity powering GPUs instead of going to waste

RELIC connects computing equipment directly to functioning solar generation sites

The system operates without grid connections or conventional data center construction

A San Francisco company named Rune has introduced a modular compute unit built to operate directly on unused solar power.

Called RELIC, the equipment attaches to functioning solar installations without needing any connection to the electrical grid or new construction work.

The launch came alongside a $40 million Series A financing round for Rune, lifting the firm's overall capital raised to $53.5 million total.

Skipping the grid bottleneck

Solar facilities routinely waste as much as 20% of the electricity they generate, adding up to more than 50 TWh yearly nationwide.

RELIC pulls that idle current straight from the source, avoiding metering charges, utility fees, and the grid limitations slowing AI growth.

"Every solar plant is a latent data center. The power is already there, sitting idle while AI labs wait years for grid connections that may never come," said William Layden, Co-Founder and CEO of Rune.

Rune states that RELIC can be installed in about 60 minutes and deliver working GPU capacity within six weeks of a contract.

That timeline contrasts sharply with conventional data center construction projects, which frequently stretch across several years before reaching full operational status.

The company reports that RELIC lowers non-compute infrastructure spending by 85%, saving roughly $620 million across a 100 MW deployment.

RELIC operates natively on direct current — solar's original output form — sidestepping energy losses that occur when converting power to alternating current.

It needs no extensive site preparation, leaves no visible trace across the landscape, and operates entirely without consuming any water.

Rune's initial working installation sits at a 200 MW solar facility located in Texas, mounted on existing infrastructure without any modifications.

Addressing a system under strain

Traditional data center construction cannot keep pace with the surging demand pouring in from artificial intelligence developers and infrastructure buyers everywhere.

Rune's approach addresses that shortfall by placing compute equipment directly beside existing renewable generation instead of pursuing new construction projects.

“Demand for AI infrastructure is growing faster than it can be delivered. Rune deploys compute directly behind the meter at operating solar farms, converting clean power into rapidly scalable AI capacity,” said Santo Politi, Founder and General Partner of Spark Capital.

“Every renewable asset in operation becomes a potential deployment site. Rune is the fastest path to new capacity we have seen."

Many data centers currently running were adapted from designs built for earlier computing needs rather than for artificial intelligence workloads specifically.

“AI’s power constraint isn’t generation, it’s resource allocation,” said Varun Palivela, Co-Founder and CTO of Rune.

“The industry is retrofitting data centers designed for a different era rather than rethinking the architecture itself. We built an entirely new technology stack from the ground up, coupling compute directly to clean generation so AI can scale here on Earth.”

The approach leaves Rune testing whether unused solar capacity can support AI computing at the speed required by growing demand.

title: Whitehouse: Call Out the Corruption Propelling the US Climate Retreat
authors: Derek Harrison, Marianne Lavelle, Alissa de Chassey
description:
A recent Inside Climate News analysis showed that specific mentions of climate change by congressional Democrats have plummeted.
“We’ve got these two horrible villains—the climate denial fraud operation … and the dark money corruption operation that the fossil fuel industry runs.
“It is a huge corrupt money pump out of the public’s pockets and into the pockets of Trump’s big fossil fuel donors,” Whitehouse said.
“Every indication is that the Supreme Court is going to obey once again the interest of the fossil fuel industry,” Whitehouse said.
With more than 100,000 climate action advocates expected to gather at the 18th annual Climate Week NYC this week, Whitehouse hopes to see them talking about the need for accountability.
text:
Democrats controlled the Senate and the presidency when Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse first sought to roust his colleagues from the chamber’s floor, warning them that they were sleep-walking into climate disaster.

Fourteen years and more than 300 “Time to Wake Up” speeches later, the Rhode Island Democrat is again prodding members of his own party—but now over a disaster that is manifest in rising costs and greater hazards across the country. In an interview with Inside Climate News in the run-up to Climate Week NYC, Whitehouse said it is more urgent than ever for fellow Democrats and climate action advocates to name the “villains”—as he repeatedly called them—who have stymied U.S. policy on the mounting global environmental crisis.

“The fossil fuel industry has done a really magnificent job of false narratives, fake science, the whole nonsense of trying to give people a way to think that they don’t have to do anything about climate change, that it’s a someday problem,” Whitehouse said. “Well, it ain’t a someday problem any longer.”

President Donald Trump’s second administration has channeled those industry narratives as it has rolled back climate protections—last week, for example, not only repealing regulations on power plant pollution, but also moving to prevent any future such rules with an official finding that greenhouse gases are not a danger to health or the environment.

As the midterm elections approach, polling shows that Trump, the Republicans and their fossil-fuel-friendly agenda are in trouble, in large part because of skyrocketing U.S. energy costs. Democrats and environmentalists have focused most of their messaging on those costs. A recent Inside Climate News analysis showed that specific mentions of climate change by congressional Democrats have plummeted.

Whitehouse maintains his colleagues are making a mistake if they aren’t talking about climate change, and about how industry money and influence on every branch of government has stymied action.

“We’re missing a big, big opportunity,” Whitehouse said, but he added, “we’ve never told the story well.”

Whitehouse began his weekly “Wake Up” speeches on climate in 2012, after the Senate’s Democratic leadership, in his view, squandered the opportunity to bring to the floor their own climate bill to match the cap-and-trade bill the House had passed in 2009, President Barack Obama’s first year in office. The Democrats would never regain the filibuster-proof majority they held for a short time—with their independent colleagues—and Trump’s election in 2016 put any hopes of climate action on the back burner.

After President Joe Biden unseated him in 2020 on a platform of rebuilding the economy with clean energy, Whitehouse was so hopeful he ended his climate floor speeches for about a year. But as he watched the scope of Biden’s climate legislation get whittled away, resulting eventually in the Inflation Reduction Act, Whitehouse took to the Senate floor again—focusing on what he felt was the missing part of the story.

“Biden refused to mention villains,” Whitehouse told Inside Climate News. “We’ve got these two horrible villains—the climate denial fraud operation … and the dark money corruption operation that the fossil fuel industry runs. And wow, how does that not become a good story that candidates can successfully tell?”

For example, he said environmental advocates need to do more than talk about how Trump’s extraordinary efforts to halt Atlantic offshore wind energy will result in less supply and therefore push electricity prices higher. They should also explain who benefits—the companies selling natural gas, oil and coal, who see more demand for their products.

“It is a huge corrupt money pump out of the public’s pockets and into the pockets of Trump’s big fossil fuel donors,” Whitehouse said. When people see high electric bills, “if they’re just mad at the electric company, we have not done our jobs,” he said.

This story is funded by readers like you.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Donate Now

If Democrats take control of the Senate in November, Whitehouse would be the most senior Democrat on the Judiciary Committee as well as on the Environment and Public Works Committee. A former U.S. attorney and attorney general of Rhode Island, Whitehouse told POLITICO last year that he would make a bid for the high-profile Judiciary spot, where he could lead the vetting of federal judicial nominees and help shape legislation to reform the Supreme Court, a step he sees as part of the climate action agenda.

He would like to see members of the high court subject to ethics rules, and has co-sponsored legislation that would establish 18-year term limits for Supreme Court justices. They’d be effective retroactively, “so you start to refresh the court right away,” he said.

In Whitehouse’s view, it was the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United decision, sweeping aside limits on corporate political donations, that allowed the fossil fuel industry to consolidate control over the Republican Party and kill hope of bipartisan climate legislation in Congress. The court went on to restrict regulatory solutions by striking down Obama’s Clean Power Plan, relying on its so-called “major questions doctrine” in 2022. And now, in Suncor v. Boulder, the first case the court will hear when its new term opens in October, Whitehouse sees a Supreme Court poised to restrict state and local government lawsuits seeking damages from the fossil fuel industry over climate change.

“Every indication is that the Supreme Court is going to obey once again the interest of the fossil fuel industry,” Whitehouse said.

The American Petroleum Institute, a frequent target of Whitehouse’s, has maintained that its member companies are committed to addressing climate change, and API’s efforts to increase oil and natural gas production are aimed at bringing down consumer costs. When Whitehouse sent a criminal referral to the U.S. Department of Justice in 2024, accusing the industry of “deception, disinformation, and doublespeak” on climate change, API called it “another unfounded political charade to distract from persistent inflation and America’s need for more energy, including oil and natural gas.”

But climate action advocates laud the steadfast role Whitehouse has played in focusing attention on the companies that have gained from climate inaction while the public pays the costs.

“He’s been a constant and invaluable thorn in the side of Big Oil and all their financial enablers,” said leading environmental activist Bill McKibben. “It’s extremely rare to see a politician stay this focused, week in and week out, on anything.”

Whitehouse also wins praise from the Republican chair of the Environment and Public Works Committee, Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, for his work as the committee’s ranking member to forge bipartisan compromise. She singled out the $35 billion Water Resources Development Act legislation—a flood risk management, drinking water and ecosystem restoration package the committee approved in July—and a permitting reform measure they are working on now.

“Senator Whitehouse has been a fantastic partner,” Capito said. “He exemplifies what it means to stand firmly by your principles while working across the aisle to find effective solutions and deliver meaningful results for the American people.”

Whitehouse sees hope in polling showing that voters—even in red states like Texas— understand that higher insurance costs are connected to climate-driven extreme weather, and the overwhelming majority of Americans believe oil and gas companies should be made to pay climate-related costs. With more than 100,000 climate action advocates expected to gather at the 18th annual Climate Week NYC this week, Whitehouse hopes to see them talking about the need for accountability.

“Are we going to end the free-to-pollute business model?” Whitehouse asked. “Are we taking seriously the potential economic catastrophe? … Are we changing the narrative so that we’re talking about costs and talking about the corruption and the villainy of the climate denial fraud and the dark money operation? If we’re doing those things, then we’re finally making some ground.”

text:
A solar-module manufacturer plans to create nearly 170 jobs at a new Summerville factory, fueled in part by U.S. tariffs being imposed on competing overseas-made products.

New York-based Translucent Energy said it's aiming to be fully operational by the end of the year at 175 McQueen Blvd., off of Jedburg Road between Interstate 26 and Highway 78.

The company, which was approved for tax breaks by Dorchester County Council on July 20, is leasing a 283,000-quare foot building previously occupied by BAE Systems, Caterpillar and Corning.

Translucent said the factory will produce solar modules for customers across the spectrum, ranging from individual homeowners to large-scale utility developers.

The $15.7 million first-phase investment is expected to create 167 jobs, "anchoring the company's plan to build a complete solar manufacturing value chain on American soil," Augustus Rylands,, managing director, said in a written statement.

The factory will make enough panels each year to create 1.2 gigawatts of energy.

"Summerville is the first step in our multiyear plan," Rylands said, adding that the company is aiming to produce solar cells and their ultra-thin wafers "in the near future."

He said the company welcomed the 15 percent tariffs announced by the Trump administration on Aug. 6 for certain foreign-made solar panel components.

The new import fees take effect Dec. 4.

"They give American solar manufacturers like us the long-term certainty needed to invest at scale," Rylands said.

Translucent said the tariffs, combined with the existing federal "45X" tax credits that are still available to clean-energy manufacturers for a few more years before being phased out, "are widely expected to accelerate the reshoring of the industry that is already underway."

Under the incentives deal that the county approved on July 20 the company's property taxes will be replaced with a fixed fee for 20 years. Also, Translucent will be credited 20 percent of those payments for six years to reimburse it for certain expenses associated with the expansion, such as road improvements and utility upgrades.

The deal surfaced publicly earlier this summer.

"For clarity, I think some folks are worried this is a solar farm," Dorchester County Council member Jay Byars said at a June 15 meeting. "It is not."

The Translucent expansion was at least the fourth to spring from the solar-energy industry in South Carolina since the spring, mostly in the Upstate.

ES Foundry, for example, recently announced an expansion of its Greenwood factory.

text:
By Molly Peterson

The burned remains of the Moss Landing Power Plant battery energy storage facility caught fire again Friday morning, prompting Monterey County officials to issue a shelter in place order — less than two years after it became one of the largest battery storage facility fires in history.

Workers for Vistra, the plant’s Texas-based operator, noticed a flare-up early Friday morning against the wall of a building that burned in the initial January 2025 fire. The cause: roughly 1,500 inaccessible battery modules, still charged, spontaneously ignited, said Chief Jess Cortez with the North County Fire Protection District.

“They’re in the smoldering stage right now,” Cortez said at a briefing Friday afternoon, adding that at that point there was no active fire. “The incident is very dynamic. There could be possible flare-ups.”

Local authorities lifted the order to shelter in place later Friday afternoon. Still, the flare-up reignites fears about battery storage facilities — even as California comes to increasingly rely on them. The state now has “the nation’s largest battery energy storage fleet,” the California Energy Commission announced in August.

“If we had only known the worst-case scenarios of how not to build batteries, we wouldn’t have built Moss Landing,” said Dustin Mulvaney, a professor at San Jose State University in the school of planning, policy and environmental studies. “Because it keeps coming back to haunt us.”

The incident also sharpens the tension between Gov. Gavin Newsom’s push to shortcut permitting for energy and other projects, and the communities hosting these facilities.

Fire, rekindled

In January 2025, residents from across the Monterey Bay area watched large plumes of smoke and ash spewing from Vistra’s 300-megawatt battery energy storage facility at the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County.

It was the facility’s fourth safety incident, the third on the Vistra property, since 2019, according to a letter Assemblymember Dawn Addis, a San Luis Obispo Democrat who represents Moss Landing and parts of Santa Cruz County, sent state regulators last year. The fire continued for days before crews could control it, then rekindled briefly a month later.

Newsom called for a state investigation. The California Public Utilities Commission began with a site visit that month.

Nearly two years later, that investigation is ongoing, with a root cause analysis underway in coordination with Vistra and an independent consultant, said Terrie Prosper, a spokesperson with the Public Utilities Commission.

Monterey County Supervisor Glenn Church expressed frustration about the delay.

“Why it takes a year and a half to come up with an answer when everything is just about near the end of being cleaned up, I don’t know,” he said.

Before the state approves any more of these facilities, he said, “it’s a good idea to know what’s causing these fires.”

Safety rules, too late

Unlike facilities built more recently, the Moss Landing site was built in an enclosed, aging building with older battery technologies crammed closely together — allowing fires to spread quickly, Mulvaney said.

Denise Grab, the Clean Energy Law & Leadership project director for the Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, agreed: The site is “one of the earlier battery storage facilities in the state and in the country, even. And the design is not up to par with current safety designs.”

Battery plants still carry less overfall harm than fossil fuel plants, Grab added.

“There are risks from other types of energy generation as well, particularly fossil fuel,” Grab said. “Asthma, premature death, heart attacks, lung disease from fossil fuel plants is significant, and (battery plants pose) a different kind of risk.”

California passed a series of safety laws both before and after the January 2025 fire, including several laws from state Sen. John Laird, a Santa Cruz Democrat, aimed at better planning for — and preventing — fires.

A 2022 law by then-Sen. Ben Hueso required the California Public Utilities Commission to set new standards for battery storage facilities and boost oversight of their emergency plans. But the commission didn’t bring its proposal for implementing Hueso’s law to a vote until after last year’s Vistra fire.

“We should have never built Moss Landing the way we did,” Mulvaney said. “We were too late with coming up with the standards and certifications, which make batteries much safer today.”

Environmental health controversy

Vistra says that the cause of last year’s fire is still unknown. The energy company commissioned a study finding that chemical concentrations in nearby soil or water posed no risk to humans or the environment.

“As a result, no further human health or ecological risk evaluation related to the (Moss Landing fire) event is warranted,” the report read.

But scientists’ findings and resident accounts suggest otherwise. As the fire blazed for days in January 2025, residents reported wheezing, coughing, headaches and eye irritation.

Researchers presented additional findings at a symposium last month, including evidence from one UC Santa Cruz researcher of elevated exposure to battery-related materials in hair samples.

Scientists with the San Jose State University’s Moss Landing Marine Laboratories have found high levels of nickel, manganese and cobalt in soil around the facility. Ivano Aiello, the scientist who led the study, said Vistra’s recent report examined potential contaminants months after the fire was contained.

The long-term health impacts of potential exposure remain unclear, and researchers continue studying the incident.

Richard Stedman, an air pollution control officer with the Monterey Bay Air Resources District, said regulators placed four monitors at the fence line around the Vistra facility, and two more nearby: None detected unhealthy levels of particulate matter as of Friday’s briefing.

Brian Roeder, founder of the community group Never Again Moss Landing, said the public’s trust in regulators and politicians who are meant to protect them continues to erode.

“We’ve had 20 months to prepare for this,” he said. “Here we are again, right back where we were before, knowing this could happen.”

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

SALISBURY — A statewide program that has certified more than 1,600 environmental educators is finding a new home at Catawba College.

The North Carolina Environmental Education Certification Program will move from the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) to Catawba’s Center for the Environment on Oct. 1.

According to a release from the Salisbury-based college, the transition will “preserve the certification program, its staff, and all the programs and resources that connect educators across the state.” That also includes the listserv and calendar.

“We ask our students to consider their stewardship as citizens, about how they can serve others,” said Catawba President David P. Nelson in the release. “We ask the same questions of the college. This program has served our state well, and we are glad to respond to this opportunity to serve the people of North Carolina by carrying on this important work.”

The certification program is part of a broader state environmental education effort that began in the early 1990s. Since the state’s July budget decision, environmental educators, classroom teachers and program partners have expressed support for continuing the work at another institution.

Lee Ball, executive director of the Center for the Environment, and staff from DEQ’s Office of Environmental Education and Public Affairs announced the transition at the 35th annual conference of Environmental Educators of North Carolina, the state’s nonprofit professional association for environmental educators. The announcement drew a standing ovation.

“This transition will extend the center’s work in environmental education and create opportunities for our students to learn from and work with educators serving communities across North Carolina,” Ball said.

DEQ Secretary Reid Wilson added, “The Environmental Education program has been a resounding success for 30 years, awarding Environmental Education Certificates to more than 1,600 people. Educating children about the natural world and their role in protecting it is more essential than ever. The Center for the Environment at Catawba College deserves a huge thanks for taking on the leadership of the program in the wake of the new state budget’s removal of its funding.”

Lisa Tolley, program manager for the environmental education program at DEQ, thanked Ball, the Center, Catawba College, Wilson, the leadership of Environmental Educators of North Carolina and the statewide community of educators for supporting the transition.

“This transition preserves North Carolina’s environmental education legacy and allows an important statewide career-development and community-building resource to continue,” Tolley said.

Marty Wiggins, program consultant for the environmental education program, said the certification program will continue to serve the entire state.

“Our plan is to make a seamless transition to the Center for the Environment,” Wiggins said. “All of the resources that support the program, such as the NCEE listserv and calendar, will continue to be an integral part of the certification program.”

Details of the Oct. 1 transition are still being finalized. Certification participants and educators who use the program’s resources are not expected to experience delays or interruptions in access.
